items.descriptionOriginal: At nearly 11,000 meters (36,089 feet) below the ocean’s surface, the Mariana Trench is a realm of crushing pressure and near-freezing darkness. Fire seems impossible here. But scientists exploring the trench’s rugged walls have uncovered evidence of the deepest explosive volcanic eruptions ever documented on Earth. The University of Texas at Dallas’s discovery upends what geologists thought was possible in one of Earth’s harshest environments. Pyroclastic flow discovered at 6,148 meters below sea level. Credit: Dr Robert J. Stern Discovery through rocks The Mariana Trench was born 52 million years ago when the Pacific tectonic plate began sliding beneath the Philippine Sea plate. Today, it holds the Challenger Deep, the deepest known valley on the ocean floor. Researchers have long wondered what drives its extraordinary depth. Seeking clues, Dr. Robert J. Stern’s team sailed to the western Pacific in late 2024 and deployed the remotely operated vehicle (ROV) Jason/Medea across a 550-kilometer (341 miles) stretch of the forearc near the Deep. Jason/Medea reached 6,500 meters (about 21,325 feet), well above the trench floor. That was still deep enough to make history. Over seven dives, the ROV revealed a geological split personality. The eastern section of the trench wall is steeper and deeper, with the boundary between Earth’s crust and upper mantle sitting closer to the seafloor. The western segment held a startling surprise. There, the team found thin, flat layers of pyroclastic rock , which is the hardened debris left behind by explosive eruptions. “Explosive volcanism near trenches is unusual, so we were very surprised,” said Stern, lead author. “These are the deepest pyroclastic rocks documented to date from anywhere in the ocean.” Stretching differently from east to west Subduction forearcs are cold. Under normal circumstances, the mantle beneath them lacks the heat required to melt and produce fresh magma. Finding young volcanic deposits there challenges long-standing tectonic assumptions. Erupting under kilometers of seawater also changes the physics of a blast. Immense hydrostatic pressure prevents volcanic gases from expanding the way they do on land or in shallow seas, muting the violent blasts seen at surface volcanoes. Still, these deep flows packed serious heat. “We haven’t identified the eruption sites yet,” said Stern. “We know that these hot pyroclastic flows moved down slopes, but we don’t think they moved very far. They retained enough heat to re-weld themselves into pretty hard rocks, and that heat would’ve been lost if the pyroclastic flows traveled great distances.” The rocks show the seafloor is stretching differently from east to west, with older eastern rocks indicating mechanical pulling and younger western volcanic rocks suggesting magma-driven expansion that researchers plan to date. At the same time, weak coupling allows the narrow Pacific plate to bend sharply and sink steeply. It explains the Challenger Deep’s extreme depth while widening the subduction zone and potentially shifting western Pacific plate motion. Still, the volcanic vents behind these pyroclastic flows remain unlocated, as reaching them requires deep-diving gear most scientists lack. “We were unable to study the seafloor between the depths of 6,500 meters and 11,000 meters, the depth of the Challenger Deep,” Stern said . “Only Chinese scientists and some wealthy entrepreneurs now have research tools capable of working down to the bottom of the Challenger Deep.” Until deeper-diving vehicles become more widely available to researchers, the fiery origins of Earth ’s darkest abyss will keep some of their secrets locked beneath the waves. The findings were published in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science.

items.descriptionOriginal: Humanoid robots have entered the combat sports arena, with a Silicon Valley event showcasing machines exchanging punches and kicks. The event, held on November 20, called REK 2.1, brought together human-shaped robots for physical bouts in front of a live audience in San Francisco. The matches highlighted how advances in robotics are enabling machines to perform increasingly dynamic movements, including striking, recovering from falls, and engaging opponents. In September, an EngineAI T800 humanoid, developed in China, fought in San Francisco at REK’s first human-versus-robot event. Humanoids trade blows Humanoid robots have taken their fighting abilities into the entertainment arena, exchanging punches, kicks, and even blade strikes in a series of combat matches in San Francisco. The demonstrations took place at REK 2.1, an event organized by Robot Entertainment Kombat (REK), which brought four humanoid robots together for three matches before an audience of about 200 people. The matches featured several humanoid robots with distinctive designs and appearances. One of the contestants was T-Rek, a robot standing approximately 180 centimeters (5.9 feet) tall, with a silver skull-like face and red eyes. Its opponent, Radar-72, featured a helmet and a brown-and-sand-colored camouflage pattern across its body. The two machines traded punches and kicks, both trying to recover quickly after being knocked to the ground. During their approximately 90-second bout, T-Rek landed a kick that left Radar-72 unable to get back up. The defeated robot was subsequently carried out of the ring on a stretcher, reports Chosun. Other contestants included Bad Boy, which featured a purple helmet with horns and green lights, and Lectile, a black-bodied humanoid with decorations resembling dreadlocks. The final match introduced another level of physical combat, with the participating robots equipped with three blades on each hand. The machines engaged in sword-fighting movements, producing metallic clashing sounds as their weapons struck each other. The robots also attempted more complex movements, including flying kicks and attacks against opponents lying on the ground. Their repeated collisions with the arena’s transparent protective panels produced loud impacts, while scratches, chipped paint, and small pieces of debris appeared during the matches. These demonstrations showcased the mechanical capabilities needed to move rapidly, maintain balance, and recover from falls during physical interactions. Unlike conventional industrial robots designed for repetitive tasks, the humanoids were configured for dynamic movements in an unpredictable combat environment. Operators control the fighting Despite the use of AI, the robots were not independently deciding how to attack or defend themselves. Human operators positioned beside the arena controlled the machines using game console-like controllers. Operators determined the robots’ movements, attack directions, defensive actions, and when to execute punches or kicks. AI-assisted systems helped the machines execute those commands while maintaining balance and controlling posture. This arrangement allows the robots to perform physically demanding movements without requiring every aspect of their balance and motion to be manually controlled. However, the demonstrations did not establish that the machines could independently plan and execute complete fighting sequences. The event also reflected the growing interest in humanoid robotics among technology workers and the wider public. Spectators watched the matches through protective panels, recording the fights and cheering for their preferred robots. According to experts, the increasing use of humanoids in physical competitions also presents new engineering and safety challenges. Robots equipped with blades or capable of delivering powerful kicks could pose risks if their movements become unpredictable or their control systems fail. The event highlighted questions surrounding the strength of protective barriers, permissible weapons, attack power, and emergency shutdown procedures. These concerns have become particularly relevant following earlier attempts to organize human-versus-robot combat events. REK previously held a September 18 match in San Francisco featuring influencer Frankie Lapenna against humanoid robots. On September 23, the California State Athletic Commission issued a notice ordering the organizers to stop unpermitted human-humanoid combat events.

Εικόνες που βλέπουν το φως της δημοσιότητας πραγματικά προκαλούν αποτροπιασμό, ενώ οι λεπτομέρειες για την κατάσταση στην οποία βρέθηκαν τα δύο ανήλικα και το πως ζούσαν σοκάρουν. Μέχρι και οι αστυνομικοί που τα εντόπισαν δυσκολεύτηκαν να συνειδητοποιήσουν τι ακριβώς βλέπουν μπροστά τους, όπως μετέδωσε η δημοσιογράφος της ΕΡΤ, Δέσποινα Κρητικού. Δείτε περισσότερα στο ertflix.gr | Ακούστε περισσότερα στο ertecho.gr Η καταγγελία για τα κλάματα Το περιστατικό αποκαλύφθηκε αργά το βράδυ του Σαββάτου (21/11), όταν η Αστυνομία ενημερώθηκε ότι από διαμέρισμα σε πολυκατοικία στους Αμπελόκηπους ακούγονταν επί αρκετή ώρα κλάματα παιδιών. Αστυνομικοί της Άμεσης Δράσης έσπευσαν στο σημείο και, έπειτα από συνεννόηση με εισαγγελέα, έσπασαν την πόρτα του διαμερίσματος . Στο εσωτερικό εντόπισαν τα δύο παιδιά μόνα τους, ενώ, σύμφωνα με τις περιγραφές των αστυνομικών, ο χώρος ήταν ιδιαίτερα ατημέλητος και δεν διέθετε καλές συνθήκες υγιεινής. Συνελήφθησαν η μητέρα και ο σύντροφός της Λίγη ώρα αργότερα, σύμφωνα με την ΕΛΑΣ, εμφανίστηκαν στο διαμέρισμα η 22χρονη μητέρα των παιδιών, από τη Συρία, και ο 25χρονος σύντροφός της, παλαιστινιακής καταγωγής, με τον οποίο συγκατοικούσε. Οι δύο ενήλικες συνελήφθησαν με την κατηγορία της έκθεσης ανηλίκων. ΡΕΠΟΡΤΑΖ ΔΕΣΠΟΙΝΑ ΚΡΗΤΙΚΟΥ www.ertnews.gr

items.descriptionOriginal: You twist open a sealed bottle of water and drink without a second thought. It's clear, it's sealed, and it's been purified. Behind that bottle is more checking than most of us realise. Since November 2024, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has treated packaged drinking water as a "high-risk" food. The label doesn't mean the water is dangerous. It means the product gets stricter scrutiny: inspections before a licence is granted, annual inspections, and regular testing of both the water and its packaging. Those checks exist because some things in water can't be seen, smelt or tasted. A recent case shows why they matter. FSSAI has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd after a water sample from its Goa plant was declared unsafe. The sample reportedly contained bromate at 12 micrograms per litre, above the limit of 10. A referral laboratory later also found polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, or PAHs. Bisleri disputes the findings. It says independent testing found bromate within the limit, that its water is safe, and that it will cooperate with the regulator. Whatever the outcome, the case raises a question most of us have never thought to ask: if water has been purified, how can chemicals linked to cancer end up in it? Here's what bromate and PAHs are, how they get into water, what levels are considered acceptable, and what the rules say about keeping them out. What happened at Bisleri's Goa plant? On 30 September 2025, FSSAI officials collected six samples from Bisleri's Goa facility. According to the company, five met the standards. The sixth showed bromate at 12 micrograms per litre, two above the limit. FSSAI has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd after a water sample from its Goa plant was declared unsafe. Photograph: (Plastic Pollution Coalition) Bisleri says it appealed on 22 November 2025, and the sample went to a referral laboratory. That lab found bromate within the limit, but detected PAHs. Bisleri also had the same sample tested at an FSSAI-approved lab, which it says found bromate within the permitted limit. It sent those results to FSSAI's Western Regional Office on 2 February 2026 . After that, the company says, it heard nothing more and assumed the matter was closed. FSSAI, however, declared the sample unsafe and sanctioned prosecution under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. It has also said it plans to test more samples from Bisleri and other packaged water companies. A prosecution sanction is not a conviction. And because the labs reported different results, it matters to separate what each test actually found from what is still disputed. How does bromate get into water? Surprisingly, bromate often comes from the very step meant to make water safe. Many bottlers disinfect water with ozone, a powerful gas that kills bacteria and viruses. But some water sources naturally contain bromide. When ozone meets bromide during treatment, the reaction can produce bromate. The World Health Organization (WHO) says this treatment process, called ozonation , is the main reason bromate shows up in drinking water. Normally, it isn't found in water in any significant amount. How much forms depends on four things: how much bromide was in the water to begin with how much ozone is used the water's pH (how acidic or alkaline it is) how long treatment runs Get the balance wrong and levels can climb. The WHO has recorded bromate anywhere from under 2 to 293 micrograms per litre in ozone-treated water. Many bottlers disinfect water with ozone, a powerful gas that kills bacteria and viruses. Photograph: (The Hospital of Central Connecticut) Bromate can also form when chlorine-based disinfectants are produced using salt that contains bromide impurities. So bromate in water doesn't necessarily mean the source was polluted. It can be a by-product of cleaning the water, which is why the treatment process itself needs close watching. How much is too much? Bromate worries scientists because it caused cancer in laboratory animals. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies potassium bromate as Group 2B, or "possibly carcinogenic to humans". Its 1999 review found strong evidence of cancer in animals, but not enough evidence in humans. That difference matters. A chemical being a possible cancer hazard doesn't mean every exposure carries the same risk. How much is present, and for how long someone is exposed, both count. The WHO's provisional limit for bromate in drinking water is 10 micrograms per litre (0.01 milligrams per litre). India's standard for packaged drinking water, BIS IS 14543:2024, also lists bromate as a chemical that must be tested. In the Bisleri case, 12 micrograms is two above the limit. That's a regulatory concern, but it doesn't mean anyone who drank the water will develop cancer or fall ill. Judging the real risk would need three things: how concentrated it was, how much someone drank, and for how long. Two things are true at once. Detecting a chemical doesn't automatically make water unsafe, because it's the amount that counts. And staying within the limit doesn't mean manufacturers can stop checking. What are PAHs, and how do they get into water? PAHs are a large family of chemicals, built from two or more linked rings of carbon atoms. They form mainly when things don't burn completely, such as coal, wood, petrol and other organic material. Vehicle exhaust, factory emissions and other burning release them into the air and the environment. PAHs don't dissolve easily in water. Instead, they tend to cling to tiny particles. According to the WHO , one known route into drinking water is the coal-tar coating used inside older water pipes to stop them corroding. Pollution from burning can also settle on soil and water, and wash into water sources as runoff. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies potassium bromate as Group 2B, or "possibly carcinogenic to humans". Photograph: (Image generated by AI) One PAH, benzo[a]pyrene, is a particular concern because it can cause cancer. The WHO's limit for it is 0.7 micrograms per litre. But PAHs are not all alike. One compound causing cancer doesn't mean they all carry the same risk. Finding PAHs in a sample also doesn't tell us how they got there. In the Bisleri case, we would need to know which compounds were found, and in what amounts, to judge how serious the finding is or where it came from. What about the plastic bottle? Bromate comes mainly from treatment, not the bottle. But scientists have looked at whether chemicals can leach from packaging into water. A 2022 study in the Bulletin of Environmental Contamination and Toxicology tested PET bottles and low-density polyethylene water packets in India. It found that the amount of plasticisers seeping into water depended on the packaging material, how long the water was stored and how hot it got. Leaching was higher at high temperatures, especially in recycled PET bottles and plastic packets. That's a good reason to pay attention to packaging and storage. But the study looked at phthalates, not bromate or PAHs, so it doesn't show that bottles caused either contaminant discussed here. What checks are already in place? Under FSSAI's 29 November 2024 order , packaged drinking water is a high-risk food category. This means: manufacturers must be inspected before they get a licence or registration inspections happen once a year centrally licensed manufacturers need an annual third-party food safety audit by an FSSAI-recognised agency From 1 January 2026, a new FSSAI testing scheme also requires manufacturers to: test their source water at FSSAI-notified, NABL-accredited labs before using it, and test any new source before it's used test for microbes every month, and for several chemicals every quarter test every parameter in the standard at least once every six months test monthly if a parameter fails, until three batches in a row pass The packaging is covered too. Bottles, jars and caps must be tested every six months for "overall and colour migration", meaning whether material or colour seeps from the packaging into the water. Manufacturers must keep these records for inspection. How does a failed sample end up in court? The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 , sets out the steps (Sections 42, 46 and 47): A Food Safety Officer collects a sample and sends it to a Food Analyst, who usually has 14 days to report. If the manufacturer disputes the result, it can appeal to the Designated Officer, who can send the sample to a referral laboratory. If the findings show a violation serious enough to prosecute, the case goes to the relevant authority for sanction. A 2022 study in the Bulletin of Environmental Contamination and Toxicology tested PET bottles and low-density polyethylene water packets in India. Photograph: (Food & Wine) In the Bisleri case, the company challenged the first result, the sample went to a referral lab, and FSSAI then sanctioned prosecution. Bisleri's independent results and its response are part of a dispute that will now be settled through the regulatory and legal process. Should consumers be worried? Chemical contaminants can't always be detected by taste, smell or look. Clear water isn't necessarily free of chemicals . But the Bisleri findings concern one regulatory sample. They don't prove that all packaged water, or every batch from the company, is unsafe. Safe drinking water depends on consistent testing and monitoring. Purification is non-negotiable, but the chemicals that can form during treatment, and contamination from storage and pipes, deserve just as much attention.

items.descriptionOriginal: When trees along a road are marked for felling, the loss extends beyond their shade and canopy. For thousands of orchids growing on their trunks and branches, the removal of a single tree can mean losing their entire habitat. In Kozhikode, Kerala, researchers faced this challenge as road-widening projects threatened mature trees supporting native orchids. Instead of allowing the plants to be lost along with the trees, they began rescuing and relocating them to other landscapes. A study published on 15 October 2026 in the scientific journal Plants has now documented the outcomes of this effort. Researchers assessed 27,324 native orchids belonging to 21 species that were relocated to three sites in Kozhikode. After monitoring them for 12 to 24 months, they found that 19,511, or 71.4%, had survived. Why roadside trees matter to orchids Unlike terrestrial orchids that grow in soil, epiphytic orchids grow on the trunks and branches of other plants. They use trees as support, relying on their bark, moisture, shade and surrounding canopy conditions to survive. When a mature host tree is felled, the orchids growing on it can lose their habitat at once. The scale of this dependence is evident from an earlier survey in Kerala. A 2025 study, Distribution and Abundance of Native Orchids on Roadside Trees in a Global Biodiversity Hotspot , recorded nearly 10,000 orchids belonging to 13 species on approximately 600 trees across Wayanad. The trees represented 72 different taxa, and the orchid population included six regional endemics. The October 2026 study notes that road construction and widening have increasingly threatened these mature host trees and the orchid communities they support. The researchers involved in the latest study included Mithun Venugopal and Pradeep N Sukumaran of the KSCSTE-Malabar Botanical Garden and Institute for Plant Sciences in Kozhikode, and Viswambharan Sarasan of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, in the UK. More than 17,000 native orchids representing 22 species had initially been transferred to Sarovaram Biopark as part of the earlier rescue programme. The subsequent effort also involved relocating orchids to two other sites: the Malabar Botanical Garden and Kappad Beach. Three sites, different survival outcomes The researchers examined how the rescued plants adapted to three distinct environments, all located in Kozhikode's coastal region. Sarovaram Biopark, an urban wetland with mangrove cover, provided a humid and relatively sheltered environment. The Malabar Botanical Garden offered a mix of shaded, marshy and moderately elevated areas. Unlike terrestrial orchids that grow in soil, epiphytic orchids grow on the trunks and branches of other plants. Photograph: (tspkumar via iNaturalist) Kappad Beach, meanwhile, exposed the orchids to stronger winds, direct sunlight and salt spray. The differences were reflected in their survival. According to the study, Sarovaram recorded the strongest overall establishment , while the exposed coastal location presented greater challenges for the plants to take root and survive. However, Kappad recorded the highest flowering rate among surviving orchids, at 35.6%. It also had the highest proportion of flowering plants producing capsules, at 62.3%. At Sarovaram, the corresponding figures were 26.3% and 34.8%, while the Malabar Botanical Garden recorded 27% and 40.1%, respectively. What the findings mean for conservation The study also examined 6,126 rescued orchids belonging to 12 regionally endemic species. Of these, 3,368 survived, translating to a survival rate of 55%. The group included eight species endemic to India and four shared between southern India and Sri Lanka. This was lower than the overall survival rate of 71.4%, highlighting the additional challenges involved in relocating species with more restricted natural distributions. The researchers found that some high-altitude and mist-forest-associated orchids also managed to survive and reproduce after being moved to lower elevations, although their establishment depended more on the receiving site. Orchids of India Calanthe biloba Lindl. #Orchids #India #Conservation #Biodiversity @ForestDeptt @Sdg13Un https://t.co/mZDyHDj2Mc — Dr. Sanjeet Kumar (Ecologist) (@BiotechSanjeet) October 19, 2026 Beyond survival, the researchers also looked at whether the rescued orchids could reproduce in their new surroundings. They found capsules containing embryos among the relocated plants , indicating that some had progressed beyond simply adapting to their new locations. However, the team stresses that relocation is not a substitute for protecting natural habitats. It is an additional conservation measure for situations where the removal of orchid-bearing trees cannot be avoided. Before a tree is marked for felling to make way for a wider road, there may be dozens of plants growing quietly on its trunk and branches. For orchids, the loss of that tree can mean the loss of an entire habitat. Identifying these plants before construction begins can make room for infrastructure without overlooking the smaller ecosystems that depend on the trees being removed. Sources: 'When Roads Remove Trees, Conservation Must Move Fast: A Rescue Translocation Model for Keralam's Native Epiphytic Orchids' : By Mithun Venugopal , Pradeep N. items.descriptionOriginal: This story is part of The Better India's new wildlife series, Species in Focus: 52 species. 52 stories. 52 reasons to protect India's wildlife. One species at a time, the series explores India's rare, endangered and lesser-known wildlife, their habitats, behaviour, ecological roles and conservation status. For years, the sight of an otter swimming through Kashmir's rivers had become rare. Once found across the Jhelum River basin, the Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra) had nearly disappeared from the valley, its numbers declining amid fur-driven poaching, habitat destruction and water pollution. Now, after decades of little evidence of its presence, the elusive mammal is being spotted again in Kashmir's waterways. A study published in the journal Biological Diversity on 23 October 2026, titled Re-Emergence of Eurasian Otter (Lutra lutra) in the Valley of Kashmir, India: A Conservation Triumph and a Challenge , documents recent sightings and field evidence of the species in the valley. Authored by Irfan Khursheed Shah and Sohail Ahmad Wagay, the study brings together reports that suggest the otter is reappearing after decades of near-local extinction. The researchers identify historical hunting for fur, habitat destruction, and water pollution as major reasons behind the species' decline. Srinagar had once served as a commercial centre for the valley's pelt and fur trade. Although wildlife protection measures introduced from the late 1970s onwards helped curb hunting and the trade, the otter population had already fallen sharply. The return was first noticed in 2025 According to the October 2026 paper, the first widely reported public evidence of the otter's return emerged in June 2025, when a video of an animal in a tributary of the Lidder River went viral. Viewers initially mistook it for a crocodile. The researchers say that professional enhancement of the footage helped establish that the animal was a Eurasian otter, a species that had become unfamiliar to many residents. For now, the recent records establish the Eurasian otter's presence in Kashmir's river systems, rather than a confirmed recovery of its population. Photograph: (IUCN Otter Specialist Group Bulletin) Following the video, camera traps were installed along the Rambiara and Lidder tributaries in July 2025. Although these did not capture the animals, researchers photographed spraints (otter droppings), which can help establish an animal's presence in an area. Another video subsequently surfaced from Ganderbal district, showing an otter feeding on a fish in the Sindh stream, another tributary of the Jhelum. Together, these records provided evidence of the animal's presence across different parts of the valley . The findings also build on earlier field research. A separate study published in the IUCN/SSC Otter Specialist Group Bulletin in January 2026 documented Eurasian otters in the Hirpora Wildlife Sanctuary, along the Rambiara River catchment in Shopian district. The Wildlife Trust of India researchers Tanushree Srivastava, Manvi Singh, Muneeb Nazir and Ishwar Narayanan, along with Sohail Ahmad Wagay of the J&K Department of Wildlife Protection, recorded an initial direct sighting during fieldwork in March 2024. They subsequently conducted a systematic survey between April and June 2025, covering a 12-km stretch of the river. The team recorded 21 signs of otter presence, including one direct sighting, spraints, pugmarks, tracks, fish-feeding remains, and camera-trap photographs. The study reported an average encounter rate of 0.34 signs per kilometre and a camera-trap capture rate of 4.31 captures per 100 trap nights. However, neither study establishes the total number of otters now living in Kashmir Valley. Why the return matters for freshwater ecosystems The Eurasian otter is classified as Near Threatened on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List. It is a semi-aquatic mammal that inhabits rivers, streams, and other freshwater environments. As a top predator, it helps regulate prey populations and is considered an indicator of freshwater ecosystem health. A separate finding from the Hirpora study also points to the importance of involving local communities in conservation. Only 15% of respondents recognised the Eurasian otter, although 92% supported its conservation. More than half reported declining fish populations in the area, indicating potential ecological pressures that also affect otter habitats. What could threaten their return? The October study cautions that the conditions in Kashmir's waterways have changed considerably since the period when otters were commonly reported. Urban expansion over paddy fields, conversion of agricultural land into apple orchards and construction along riverbanks have reduced and fragmented potential habitats. The decline in traditional irrigation canals has further affected the network of waterways available to the animals. The researchers also identify river pollution from heavy metals, pesticides, microplastics, and plastic waste as potential threats. Destructive fishing practices involving chemicals and electric currents, human disturbance and the increasing presence of stray dogs could further affect their survival. We are into the middle stage of our '13 Weeks of Otters' series, and next up we have one that the IOSF are very familiar with, the Eurasian Otter! Photo by Terry Evans! #Conservation #Eurasian #Otter #Wild https://t.co/NBY5RQ0ZNR https://t.co/CklFyxizXv — International Otter Survival Fund (IOSF) (@IOSF) August 8, 2022 Climate change presents another challenge. Changes in water levels, floods, landslides and prolonged dry spells can damage or expose the sheltered riverbank spaces, known as holts, where otters rest and raise their young. The researchers also flag the possibility of conflict with expanding trout farms , which are an increasingly important source of livelihood in the valley. What conservation efforts need to focus on The October 2026 paper recommends a coordinated conservation plan involving researchers, wildlife authorities and conservation organisations. This includes protecting and improving river habitats, addressing pollution, preventing hunting and monitoring the species across its newly documented locations. It also calls for public awareness campaigns to address misconceptions about otters. The researchers recommend educational initiatives in schools, awareness material in local languages and outreach at tourist destinations to help residents recognise the species and understand its behaviour. The authors note that otter encounters rarely result in harm to humans globally, and that most interactions are neutral. Better public understanding, therefore, is an important part of ensuring the animals can persist in waterways shared with people. For now, the recent records establish the Eurasian otter's presence in Kashmir's river systems, rather than a confirmed recovery of its population. Sustained monitoring and protection of these freshwater habitats will be necessary to determine whether the species can establish a lasting presence in the valley. Sources: 'Re‐Emergence of Eurasian Otter ( Lutra Lutra ) in the Valley of Kashmir, India: A Conservation Triumph and a Challenge' : By Irfan Khursheed Shah, Sohail Ahmad Wagay, Published in October 2026 'Eurasian Otters Make Remarkable Re-Emergence In Kashmir Valley After Decades-Long Absence' : By Eurasia Review, Published on 8 November 2026 'An Overview on Lutra lutra' : By Seyed Parsa Mousavi, Mohammad Mahdi Ramzanipour, and Mohammad Forouhar Vajargah, Published on 15 April 2023 'The Satpura Otter Saga' : By Raza Kazmi, Wildlife Conservation Trust, Published in December 2024

Το πρόγραμμα ενισχύει την ισότιμη πρόσβαση σε υπηρεσίες υγείας και πρόληψης σε απομακρυσμένες περιοχές της χώρας και παράλληλα υποστηρίζει πρωτοβουλίες που καλύπτουν ουσιαστικές ανάγκες των τοπικών κοινωνιών. «Μαζί, με στόχο την υγεία» δίνουν ραντεβού για αιμοδοσία στο Δημοτικό Ιατρείο Ναυπλίου την Τετάρτη 25 Νοεμβρίου , 09:30-13:00 και την Τετάρτη 2 Δεκεμβρίου , 09:00-13:30, στον Πολυχώρο «Ρεγγίνα» του Δημοτικού Πνευματικού Κέντρου Καλαμάτας, με την αιγίδα της Περιφέρειας Πελοποννήσου και του Δήμου Ναυπλιέων. Η αιμοδοσία πραγματοποιείται σε συνεργασία με το Γενικό Νοσοκομείο Αργολίδας και το Γενικό Νοσοκομείο Καλαμάτας, με στόχο την ενίσχυση των αποθεμάτων αίματος και την κάλυψη των καθημερινών αναγκών ασθενών που χρειάζονται μετάγγιση . Η ομάδα του Bloode θα βρίσκεται στον χώρο για να υποδεχθεί και να καθοδηγήσει τους συμμετέχοντες σε κάθε στάδιο της διαδικασίας και παράλληλα θα πραγματοποιηθεί δράση ενημέρωσης και εγγραφής εθελοντών δοτών μυελού των οστών για όσους το επιθυμούν, με την υποστήριξη του ΜΚΟ Choose Life και του Συλλόγου «Αρχέγονο Κύτταρο Αίματος». Στο πλαίσιο της δράσης, το Bloode θα οργανώσει ενημερωτικές δράσεις για την αξία της τακτικής εθελοντικής αιμοδοσίας , σε τοπικά σχολεία, εκπαιδευτικά ιδρύματα ανώτατης εκπαίδευσης, τοπικούς φορείς και οργανισμούς, ενδυναμώνοντας το πνεύμα προσφοράς στις τοπικές κοινωνίες. Η ανάγκη για αίμα είναι διαρκής . Με μία μόνο αιμοδοσία, που διαρκεί περίπου 20 λεπτά, ένας εθελοντής αιμοδότης μπορεί να συμβάλει στη βοήθεια έως και 3 συνανθρώπων μας. Μπορείτε να κλείσετε το ραντεβού σας, ΕΔΩ . Ειδήσεις σήμερα Κέιτ Μίντλετον: «Ο καρκίνος σε αλλάζει» – Η προσωπική της αφήγηση σε νέο ντοκιμαντέρ Αντιγήρανση και μακροζωία: Φρένο στις «θαυματουργές» θεραπείες βάζει το υπουργείο Υγείας – Τι αλλάζει Χάος στις εφημερίες των νοσοκομείων της Αττικής – Πρόβλημα χωρίς λύση το «Αττικόν»

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Baby Elephant Rescue Zuri Thrives Months After Septic Tank Ordeal Reading Time: 3 minutes Baby elephant rescue Zuri has thrived for months at the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust’s Nairobi Nursery after nearly drowning in a septic tank in Kenya. Baby elephant rescue stories rarely end as well as Zuri’s. Found trapped inside a septic tank near Voi Safari Lodge in Kenya when she was just days old, the calf has spent the past months recovering at the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust’s nursery in Nairobi. Keepers now describe a confident, food-driven toddler who has already claimed the role of herd princess. Rescuers worked late into the night to free Zuri from the tank, a traumatic ordeal for any elephant calf, let alone one only days old. After a night of stabilization at the Trust’s nearby Voi facility, she was flown to the Nairobi Nursery for round-the-clock care. The Nairobi Nursery is the first stop in a rehabilitation journey that can stretch for more than a decade. Orphaned elephants typically arrive after losing their mothers to poaching, drought, conflict, or accidents like Zuri’s. Keepers assign each calf a dedicated human caregiver who stays close around the clock, standing in for the mother an orphan has lost. Each baby elephant rescue brings its own logistical demands. Calves depend on a specialized milk formula that took decades of trial and error to perfect, since cow’s milk alone proved fatal to earlier generations of rescued elephants. Round-the-clock bottle feeding, veterinary monitoring, and a rotating team of keepers all continue for months or years after a calf first arrives. Within days of arriving, Zuri settled into the nursery herd and quickly displaced an older calf as the group’s most doted-on member. Several older orphans now compete to shepherd her around, with one in particular walking her into her stable each evening for weeks, until Zuri felt ready to go in alone. Keepers describe Zuri as anything but timid. She reportedly bangs on her stable door the moment she hears a wheelbarrow of milk bottles approaching at night, and sprints toward keepers with her trunk raised during the day, visibly displeased if a bottle isn’t ready and waiting. She has even tried stealing bottles from an older herd mate after finishing her own. Despite her boldness, Zuri shows a softer side around the nursery’s newest arrival, a recently rescued calf not yet publicly introduced. Keepers say Zuri doesn’t treat the newcomer as a rival the way she does with some of the older toddlers, a distinction they see as a promising sign of her continued emotional development. Bold enough to bang on her stable door at feeding time and steal milk bottles from herd mates, Zuri also shows a gentler side with the nursery’s newest arrival, a sign keepers read as promising emotional growth in the baby elephant rescue. Photo courtesy of Sheldrick Wildlife Trust . Not every trace of the ordeal has faded. Zuri remains wary of unfamiliar people and some of her own keepers, a caution the Trust attributes to her brush with drowning and the fear she experienced during the traumatic rescue. Recovery from early trauma varies widely between individual elephants, and keepers say patience, gentle care, reassurance, and close observation, rather than a fixed timeline, guide each calf’s progress. Over time, they hope Zuri will continue building confidence and feel increasingly secure in her new environment. Zuri’s progress reflects decades of institutional experience behind this kind of baby elephant rescue work. The Sheldrick Wildlife Trust has run its elephant rescue and rehabilitation program since the 1970s, hand-raising hundreds of orphans and successfully returning most to wild herds in Tsavo. Public support directly funds this kind of work. Individual donors can foster a specific orphan, supporting a program that covers keeper salaries, milk formula, and veterinary costs for calves like Zuri. That funding model has let the Trust scale its operations even as new rescue calls keep coming in from across Kenya. Around three years old, Zuri will eventually graduate from the nursery to one of the Trust’s reintegration units in Tsavo, following the same path generations of orphans before her took. For now, her days are filled with milk, mischief, and the attention of a devoted entourage of nannies. For a calf whose baby elephant rescue began three months ago with a near-drowning in a septic tank, that counts as a very good life. The post Baby Elephant Rescue Zuri Thrives Months After Septic Tank Ordeal appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: A s a taxi driver, Juan Barbosa should in theory be one of the strongest opponents of a crackdown on cars. But, puffing on a cigarette beside his vehicle on a sultry August afternoon, the inhabitant of Pontevedra, Spain, admits that he finds himself in something of an existential crisis. “As a driver, I suffer,” says Barbosa, who has been ferrying passengers around the northwestern city for two decades. “We can’t enter certain areas unless we have a customer or a booking. We have to take longer routes. But as a pedestrian, life is better. I enjoy it when there are fewer vehicles around.” Post-pandemic, pedestrian-first urban planning is now all the rage, from 15-minute cities to low-traffic zones and the rise of soft mobility ( human-powered or low-emission electric transport). But Pontevedra, which is home to 85,000 people in the city and just under a million in the province, was way ahead of the curve. It technically began its war on cars last century. (In 1999, to be precise.) The urban transformation of Pontevedra was carried out gradually, over the course of several years. Credit: Peter Yeung Today Pontevedra, which fittingly is located on one of the world-famous Camino de Santiago pilgrimage routes , is considered perhaps the greatest example in the world when it comes to getting rid of cars. Every year, delegations of mayors, professors and city planners make their own pilgrimage to learn about this great vanishing act. “Pontevedra is an influential example and something we speak of often,” says Mark Nieuwenhuijsen , director of the urban planning, environment and health initiative at ISGlobal, a public health research institute based in Barcelona. “Many cities are now following their direction: It reduces air pollution, noise, and livability improves.” Over the course of the 20th century, the city came to be dominated by vehicles. By the late 1990s, an average of 80,000 cars drove through Pontevedra every day — astonishingly, according to the municipality, three times more than through Madrid and five times more than London. Many of these vehicles weren’t even heading for the city, but rather transiting to other destinations such as beach towns on the coast. Those that did stay would turn the city’s charming historic squares into parking lots. Pontevedra before it was redesigned for pedestrians. Credit: Council of Pontevedra This came at a cost. Pontevedra’s epoch of cars dirtied the air, led to the deaths of pedestrians and seized centuries-old public spaces from residents. “The city was loud, disagreeable, unlivable,” says Miguel Anxo Fernández Lores, the longstanding mayor of Pontevedra, from the desk of his city hall office. “All the roads were filled with cars. The city was like a huge, permanent traffic jam.” Fernández Lores, a doctor by trade, decided enough was enough. In 1999, he campaigned to reclaim Pontevedra’s streets. The population agreed and elected him. Yet the urban transformation was not overnight. It has been carried out gradually. Fernández Lores began with a major effort to keep unnecessary cars out of the historic city center, removing significant amounts of on-street parking and only allowing essential vehicles to enter. Within one month in office, he had pedestrianized 300,000 square meters of the city center. In other parts of the city, he narrowed roads and widened sidewalks, introduced 30 kilometer per hour speed limits citywide, down from 50 kilometers per hour, and began installing traffic-calming measures like raised pedestrian crosswalks as well as almost 300 speed bumps. To take one example, the central Benito Corbel Street once had four lanes of traffic. In 2000, that was reduced to two lanes with widened sidewalks and trees. By 2014, it became a single-track road with only service vehicles able to enter, and even then for a limited time. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] The mayor, who passed a Traffic and Mobility Plan for Pontevedra in 2011 formalizing and defining his pedestrian-first approach, also developed infrastructure to make it easier to ditch cars. The city now has roughly 4,500 private underground parking spaces and about 3,500 free “park and ride” spaces, all within a short walking distance from the center. Traffic lights were replaced by roundabouts to facilitate the flow of the remaining vehicles. In some central areas, the speed limit was lowered to just 10 kilometers per hour. Trees, green spaces and street lighting were also added to improve livability. But despite its reputation, Pontevedra is not completely car-free — it allows certain vehicles on its streets within reason. “It’s not a city without cars,” says Fernández Lores. “But we only let the ones that really need to come here in.” Miguel Anxo Fernández Lores, the longstanding mayor of Pontevedra. Credit: Peter Yeung Residents can drive to garaged parking spots in the city. People with disabilities are free to drive in Pontevedra as long as they have a permit. And vehicles used for emergencies and public services such as garbage and water trucks and ambulances are permitted 24/7. Home deliveries, house moving and loading and unloading by businesses are allowed, but only during certain hours. And indeed, taxi drivers like Barbosa may enter certain zones if they have a client or booking. When necessary, police can issue fines of several hundred euros, ensuring these limits are respected. “I think it was very smart, the decisions they made,” says Mirian Calvo , a researcher and expert in urban design from Pontevedra. “And this philosophy, of mixed-traffic, prioritizing soft mobility, has been applied over 30 years, more or less.” The results of Pontevedra’s policy to prioritize pedestrians in public spaces, sustained over more than a quarter of a century, are nothing short of stunning. Car trips in the city center have fallen by 97 percent, according to official municipal figures. The air is markedly cleaner, with CO2 emissions dropping by about 70 percent. And the streets are much safer: There have been no traffic deaths since 2011, whereas between 1996 and 2006, 30 people died in traffic accidents. (Pontevedra has won European road safety awards in the process.) The streets of Pontevedra have gotten much safer: There have been no traffic deaths since 2011. Credit: Pilar Picas / Shutterstock In fact, about 90 percent of all journeys in the city center are by foot, with road safety so high that 80 percent of kids aged 6 to 12 walk without their parents to school each morning. Many local business owners have signed up to be supervisors if the children need help for any reason. For all the talk of the climate and safety benefits that come with limiting vehicle traffic and designing pedestrian-first urban spaces, however, there has been a surprising further advantage: Pontevedra is thriving economically. While in the 1990s, retail activity was drifting towards the suburbs, the decision to prioritize a compact, walkable city with a high quality of life, has changed the picture drastically. The mayor, for his part, has rejected proposals to build malls on the urban periphery, protecting the pedestrian-oriented urban core. “We don’t want huge malls, we want small, independent businesses,” says Fernández Lores. Pontevedra is now the fastest-growing city in the region of Galicia and in recent years has attracted 15,000 new inhabitants, mostly young families from elsewhere in northwest Spain. It also generates more jobs per capita than any other city in the region. The results of Pontevedra’s policy to prioritize pedestrians in public spaces, sustained over more than a quarter of a century, are nothing short of stunning. Credit: Peter Yeung “It’s a very convenient city now,” says Calvo. “It’s a very nice city to live in and people can see that.” Most locals are effusive in their praise. Esther Louzao, 68, says that her home near Plaza Pelegrina was once surrounded by cars, but not anymore. She has even stopped driving to work, instead opting to go by bus. But she keeps her car for beach days. “I like it a lot, it’s easier to walk,” says Louzao, fittingly waiting at a bus stop. Pacing down the street with a stroller, Anna, a 39-year-old with a toddler son who lives four kilometers out of town, agrees. “It’s better, much safer, it’s pleasant,” she explains. “Even if sometimes my journeys take a bit longer.” Yet not all residents are entirely convinced by the policy. Manuel, who has been living in Pontevedra for 40 years, believes the transformation has been overstated. He owns three cars: one for the city, one for going to the beach and a third for sport driving. “Yes, the city is a lot different to how it was before,” says Manuel. “But it’s not as perfect as it seems. Some of us still need cars.” In Spain, all municipalities with over 50,000 inhabitants are now required have a low emission zone, like this one in Santander. Credit: Scharfsinn / Shutterstock Calvo agrees, noting that Pontevedra’s public transit network is lacking, which means that elderly people suffer and that cars must be taken to the coastal beaches. A system like Rome’s fleet of electric minibuses in the historic center could be implemented, she says. And although the results of Pontevedra’s policy are hard to deny, Calvo, who is also a lecturer in participatory architecture, argues that the system could have been even more effective and popular if residents had been more involved in the process. In the 2000s, she says, there was significant opposition to the project, even if that has now disappeared due to the clearly positive impact. “I don’t think there has been serious public engagement,” she says. “There are more things that could be done to make it more participatory.” Nieuwenhuijsen, however, commends Pontevedra’s less confrontational approach, which presented the restriction of cars as about livability. “I think everyone would prefer places with less noise and less pollution,” he says. “It shouldn’t be about the war on cars, presented as punishing someone.” In 2019, Oslo became the first European capital to effectively make its city center car-free. Credit: OlgaVysh / Shutterstock In any case, cities across the world are following in Pontevedra’s pioneering footsteps. In 2019, Oslo became the first European capital to effectively make its city center car-free by removing on-street parking spaces and restricting access. Freiburg, Germany, has similarly transformed the district of Vauban into a car-free zone, banning on-street parking and introducing vehicle speed limits at walking pace on residential streets. And in 2022, the Spanish government approved a royal decree requiring all municipalities with over 50,000 inhabitants to have a low emission zone, and recommending the use of traffic-restricted areas like that of Pontevedra. Yet not every place can easily replicate Pontevedra’s success. Professor Nieuwenhuijsen admits the transformation of North American cities could be more challenging given their size and lack of density. “U.S. cities were built around the car,” he says. “You get a lot of sprawl. European cities are different, many were designed for walking and horse carriages.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Likewise, transforming larger cities will not be as easy. Redesigning urban areas could be slowed or halted by infrastructure such as underground piping, adds Nieuwenhuijsen, and the investment required could prove prohibitive. Barcelona’s Superblocks cost as little as €500,000 but as much as €10 million per unit in some cases. But Fernández Lores, who is planning to run for an eighth term in 2027, believes that bigger cities could begin shifting away from cars and towards pedestrians by focusing on districts rather than entire cities. A case in point: In 2023, Culdesac Tempe, Arizona, became the first purpose-built, entirely car-free residential neighborhood in the U.S. “Cities work without cars,” he says. “But each city must find its own way.” The post The City That Kicked Out Cars Before It Was Cool appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: A U.S. intelligence assessment says Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon, a capability the Defense Intelligence Agency warns could damage or disable thousands of satellites at once, Space.com reported Nov. 20. The finding appears in the DIA’s 2026 “Challenges to Security in Space,” the agency’s third unclassified report on the topic. Its information is current as of July 2026, and it covers China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea. What a nuclear blast in orbit could do “A space-based capability such as this could cause rapid and sudden loss or degradation of thousands of satellites operated by countries and companies around the world,” the report states, along with the communications, navigation, scientific, meteorological, commercial and national security services they provide. A detonation could be tailored to affect most orbits, the report says: low Earth orbit, home to commercial and reconnaissance satellites; geosynchronous orbit, used for critical communications; and medium Earth orbit , used for navigation and timing. Russia is pursuing the capability despite its obligations under the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bars placing objects carrying nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit. Moscow has previously denied developing a nuclear weapon for space. A wider toolkit of counterspace threats The nuclear satellite is one item on a longer list. The DIA says China and Russia are building “a formidable spectrum” of ways to degrade or destroy other nations’ space services. It sorts counterspace tools into four groups. Antisatellite missiles strike satellites directly and can leave debris in orbit for decades or centuries. Physical or cyberattacks hit ground sites and the data flowing to and from satellites. Electronic attacks , including jamming and spoofing, target a nation’s use of the radio spectrum. Directed-energy weapons can temporarily or permanently blind imaging satellites or affect infrared and weather sensors. Some of these effects are reversible, and others are not. The DIA notes that cheaper, smaller, simpler satellites and expanding commercial launch services are speeding the use of commercial space for national security. That same availability, it adds, extends to state and non-state actors with malign interests. Beyond Earth orbit The report also looks at cislunar space, the region between Earth and the Moon. China has stated a goal of building a cislunar space economy by 2045 and is the first country to attempt sustained operations on the Moon’s far side, the report says. China portrays its interest as peaceful, but Chinese officials have discussed pursuing military capabilities there. Peter Garretson, a senior fellow in defense studies at the American Foreign Policy Council, told Space.com that the most significant change from earlier DIA assessments is the explicit judgment about Russia’s nuclear-armed satellite . He said it reflects concern in Congress and the Trump White House. He also flagged an omission: the 2022 report’s treatment of research competition and the potential military use of deep space has disappeared. The outlook The DIA expects space to stay increasingly competitive and crowded. The growth of Chinese, Russian, Iranian and North Korean counterspace capabilities, the rapid rise in space objects and the demand for space-enabled services, it says, “will all complicate operations in space in the coming decade.”

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Meet the Southeastern Gentoo, a New Penguin Species Discovered on the Kerguelen Islands Reading Time: 3 minutes Genomes from 64 gentoo penguins show the familiar bird is really four species, including the southeastern gentoo, a new penguin species discovered on the Kerguelen Islands. New penguin species discovered on the Kerguelen Islands? It is rare news in the penguin world. Yet the southeastern gentoo penguin is the first living penguin species named in more than a century. The Kerguelen Islands are a remote, windswept French territory in the southern Indian Ocean. Gentoo penguins have nested there for thousands of years. Until now, no one realized the local birds were their own species. Gentoos are easy to spot. They have a white patch above each eye and a bright orange bill. They are also among the fastest-swimming penguins. For more than a century, scientists treated all gentoos as one widespread species. Some proposed as many as six subspecies, but experts never agreed. A new genetic study now settles the debate. Communications Biology published the study in September 2026. Daly Noll, a graduate student at the University of Chile, led the genetic analysis. Senior authors came from Andrés Bello National University in Chile and the University of California, Berkeley. The team sequenced the full genomes of 64 penguins from 10 breeding colonies. Those colonies span almost the entire gentoo range. The researchers also compared body size, calls, diets, and breeding schedules. Scientists from about a dozen countries helped identify the new penguin species discovered on the Kerguelen Islands. Contributors came from Australia, South Africa, France, Brazil, and beyond. The data revealed four distinct species. The northern gentoo lives on the Falkland Islands and near South America. The eastern gentoo breeds on Crozet, Marion, and Macquarie islands. The southern gentoo occupies the Antarctic Peninsula, coastal Antarctica, and South Georgia. The fourth is the southeastern gentoo ( Pygoscelis kerguelensis ). It lives on the Kerguelen Islands and probably on nearby Heard Island too. Biologists call the southeastern gentoo a cryptic species. It looks almost identical to its relatives, and its differences lie mainly in its genes. Its body size and calls also differ subtly. This new penguin species discovered on the Kerguelen Islands has a relatively small population. That makes accurate classification especially important for its protection. The four species began to split between 300,000 and 500,000 years ago. Island isolation played a major role. The Antarctic Polar Front, an ocean boundary where water temperature and salinity change sharply, also played a role. Island isolation and the Antarctic Polar Front helped drive the evolution of four distinct species over hundreds of thousands of years. Photo by Antoine Lamielle on Wikimedia Commons. Gentoos also tend to return to the same colonies year after year. Over time, this loyalty to home kept populations apart. Each group then adapted to its own conditions. A flexible diet helped too. Gentoos eat fish, krill, squid, and cuttlefish, so each population could thrive on whatever its local waters offered. The genomes show those adaptations clearly. Southern gentoos carry genes for heat production and fat storage, while eastern gentoos carry genes for diving. Northern gentoos carry genes linked to digestion and heart function. Dr. Jane Younger of the University of Tasmania first proposed the split in a 2020 paper. Her team later examined museum specimens and found consistent physical differences between regions. She says the new study provides in-depth evidence to support that claim. Why does this matter beyond the name? Treating gentoos as one species produced an overall positive trend. That average hid serious declines in some regions. Southern gentoos on the Antarctic Peninsula are thriving and spreading south. In the Falklands, avian influenza has hit northern gentoos hard in recent years. Populations on Macquarie Island are declining. Climate change raises the stakes for each species. Under a moderate warming scenario, sub-Antarctic gentoos could lose suitable habitat on all their current islands by 2050. Few nearby islands offer alternatives. Antarctic gentoos may fare better and could even expand their range. Emperor, Adélie, and chinstrap penguins, however, are expected to decline as sea ice shrinks and krill supplies change. Other threats include warming seas, introduced rats and dogs, competition with fisheries, and capture in fishing gear. Recognizing each species allows conservation plans to match the threats each one faces. Researchers are already taking next steps. Senior author Juliana Vianna is studying penguin genomes for traits linked to surviving avian influenza. The team has also asked taxonomic authorities to review the split formally. Conservation bodies will need to assess each species separately. That work will determine how much protection the new penguin species discovered on the Kerguelen Islands receives. A bird seen in countless photos and documentaries turned out to hold hidden diversity . Careful genetic work revealed it. The new penguin species discovered on the Kerguelen Islands shows how much remains to be learned about familiar wildlife. The post Meet the Southeastern Gentoo, a New Penguin Species Discovered on the Kerguelen Islands appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: A classroom fan spins above a group of children bent over their notebooks. As the teacher moves between desks and lessons continue, the fan keeps the air circulating. But in a city like Delhi, where pollution often makes its way indoors, circulating air does not necessarily mean breathing clean air. Project Vayu's balloon-shaped filter fits over ordinary table and wall fans, helping capture fine particulate matter from classroom air. For thousands of children studying in schools that cannot afford expensive air purifiers, this is an everyday reality. They spend several hours a day inside classrooms, often with little protection from fine particulate matter suspended in the air. Two Delhi teenagers, Krish Aggarwal and Samarth Meattle, decided to look at this problem differently. Instead of asking schools to invest in expensive purification systems, they wondered if the fans already fitted in classrooms could be made to do more. Their idea took shape as Project Vayu, an initiative that has developed an affordable filter that fits over ordinary table and wall fans, helping turn them into air purifiers. At approximately Rs 140 per filter, the innovation offers schools a way to tackle indoor air pollution without having to invest in entirely new equipment. "Growing up in Delhi, we've personally experienced the effects of air pollution," the duo say. "What bothered us was that while some schools could afford expensive air purifiers, thousands of students in under-resourced schools had no protection." What if a classroom fan could also clean the air? Rather than building a new appliance from scratch, Krish and Samarth decided to work with the infrastructure schools already had. The biggest technical challenge was developing a filter that could trap fine particulate matter, particularly PM2.5, without restricting the airflow of an ordinary fan. "We experimented with different designs before arriving at our balloon-shaped filter, made from electret media with electrostatically charged fibres," they explain. The filter uses electrostatically charged fibres that attract and capture tiny airborne particles. It fits over an existing table or wall fan with the help of an elastic lining. Once the fan is switched on, the airflow inflates the filter into a balloon-like shape, increasing its surface area for filtration. There is no need for additional motors, electrical modifications or specialised installation. The filter can be fitted in under a minute, without tools. To develop and test the technology , the teenagers approached Hollingsworth & Vose, a filtration media manufacturer. They initially emailed the company's India team with their idea and were surprised by its willingness to support them. The company provided filtration media free of cost and collaborated with the team on research and development. Priced at approximately Rs 140, the filter offers under-resourced schools an affordable alternative to expensive air purification systems. "The technology to clean air already exists. Schools just can't afford it. By using fans that classrooms already have, we eliminated the need for expensive motors and additional infrastructure," they say. This support has helped keep the manufacturing cost at approximately Rs 140 per filter. What difference can a Rs 140 filter make? For the young innovators , developing an affordable product was only half the task. They also needed to establish whether it could make a measurable difference to indoor air quality. According to the founders, independent and external testing, along with joint research and development with Hollingsworth & Vose, has produced encouraging results. In a closed room measuring approximately 200 square feet, PM2.5 concentrations reportedly dropped from 158 to 11 micrograms per cubic metre within an hour of using the filter, a reduction of over 90%. The results, however, depend on the room's size and conditions. In a larger classroom, the team recorded a 60% reduction in PM2.5 levels over an hour, with further reductions over several hours of use. There is also a visible reminder of the particles being trapped. "One of the most striking things is seeing the filters turn from white to grey or even black after a few weeks of use. It's a visible reminder of just how much particulate pollution is present in classrooms," they say. From 295 classrooms to thousands of students Getting schools to trust an unfamiliar technology developed by high school students was not easy. Project Vayu began with a pilot covering 295 classrooms and around 8,000 students. It has since reached approximately 20,000 students across more than 10 schools. Initially, many institutions were understandably hesitant. Demonstrations and explanations of the testing behind the filters, however, helped the team build confidence. Project Vayu began with a pilot covering 295 classrooms and approximately 8,000 students. The initiative has since expanded to more than 10 schools and has reached around 20,000 students. The team has also installed filters in several under-resourced medical clinics. Their work has not been without challenges. Identifying schools, securing permissions and navigating institutional processes have often slowed installations. "Balancing Project Vayu with academics has definitely been challenging. A lot of our time goes into approaching schools, coordinating installations, and following up on approvals," they say. The effort has also brought recognition. Krish was named to the 2026 Diana Award Roll of Honour for his work with Project Vayu. For him, the recognition belongs to everyone who helped build the initiative, including Samarth and their collaborators. "Project Vayu has taught me that innovation doesn't always require inventing something entirely new. Sometimes it's about making existing technology more accessible," Samarth adds. What's next for Project Vayu? The duo now hopes to expand Project Vayu to more schools across Delhi and eventually other parts of India. They are keen to work with government bodies, school principals, teachers and organisations that can help take the filters to children who need them. Their ambition is rooted in a simple belief: access to cleaner air should not depend on how much a school can spend. For Krish and Samarth, the idea was never just about making a fan work differently. It was about looking at something already available in classrooms and asking how it could serve children better. And sometimes, making a difference does not require an entirely new machine. It begins with finding a new purpose for something that is already there. Με επικεφαλής τον καθηγητή ZHANG Tianlong, Επίκουρο Καθηγητή στο Τμήμα του HKUST o…
items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) have developed an innovative titanium alloy design strategy that could pave the way for stronger, more durable materials for aerospace, automotive, biomedical and other advanced engineering applications. Led by Prof. ZHANG Tianlong, Assistant Professor in HKUST’s Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, the research team has introduced a novel approach based on three-dimensional (3D) compositional waves enabled by additive manufacturing. The technique uses in-situ alloying during laser powder bed fusion, a metal 3D-printing process, to create interconnected, microscale variations in molybdenum (Mo) concentration within the widely used Ti-6Al-4V titanium alloy. Titanium alloys are used for their high strength-to-weight ratio The research, titled “Compositional architecting by additive manufacturing enables hardenable titanium alloys,” was recently published in the prestigious journal Nature Communications. Titanium alloys are valued across several industries for their high strength-to-weight ratio, excellent corrosion resistance and, in biomedical applications, strong biocompatibility. Despite these advantages, conventional titanium alloys generally have limited strain-hardening capabilities. Strain hardening allows a material to become stronger as it undergoes plastic deformation. When this capability is insufficient, deformation tends to concentrate in specific regions, a phenomenon known as strain localization. This can compromise a material’s ability to withstand further loading and limit its reliability in safety-critical applications. HKUST team explored a fundamentally different approach to alloy design To address this challenge, the HKUST team explored a fundamentally different approach to alloy design. Instead of pursuing a chemically uniform composition, they deliberately introduced spatial variations in alloying elements to control how different parts of the material respond to mechanical stress. Using additive manufacturing, the researchers created interconnected 3D compositional waves of molybdenum within the Ti-6Al-4V alloy, producing three distinct regions with different phase stabilities and deformation characteristics. Each region contributes a different deformation mechanism when the material is subjected to mechanical loading. Low-molybdenum regions contain cooling-induced α’ martensite and deform through detwinning and retwinning. Medium-molybdenum regions contain a metastable β phase, which progressively transforms into martensite under applied stress. Meanwhile, high-molybdenum regions feature a stable β phase and primarily deform through dislocation slip. Mechanisms work together Crucially, these mechanisms work together rather than independently. Their interactions generate heterogeneous-deformation-induced (HDI) stresses, allowing different deformation mechanisms to become active progressively as the applied stress increases. This sequential and cooperative response helps maintain strain hardening over a wider range of deformation, delaying strain localization and improving the alloy’s ability to withstand mechanical loading. The resulting Ti64-6Mo alloy demonstrated impressive mechanical properties, highlighting the potential of this new design strategy. The material achieved a strain-hardening increment of approximately 557 MPa, more than twice the typical upper limit reported for conventional titanium alloys. It also recorded a tensile strength of 1,236 MPa and a uniform elongation of 11.5%. These results demonstrate that carefully engineered compositional variations can improve the combination of strength and deformation resistance, offering a promising route towards titanium alloys with enhanced mechanical performance. Challenging the traditional approach The study challenges the traditional approach to alloy development, which has largely emphasized achieving homogeneous chemical compositions throughout a material. Instead, the HKUST research demonstrates that chemical heterogeneity can be a valuable design feature. By controlling the spatial distribution of alloying elements, researchers can tailor phase stability and coordinate multiple deformation mechanisms within a single material. Commenting on the significance of the findings, Prof. Zhang said, “This study shows that alloy design does not have to focus solely on the overall uniform chemical composition. By controlling how alloying elements are distributed in three-dimensional space, we can coordinate multiple deformation mechanisms within a single material. Compositional architecting opens up an extra degree of freedom for designing the next generation of high-performance structural alloys.” The concept of compositional architecting could have implications beyond titanium alloys. Its potential extension to other advanced structural materials may open new opportunities for developing materials with tailored mechanical properties for demanding engineering applications. By combining additive manufacturing with three-dimensional compositional control, the HKUST team has demonstrated a new direction in materials engineering—one in which the strategic arrangement of chemical elements becomes as important as the overall composition in determining material performance.

items.descriptionOriginal: Astronomers may be one step closer to solving one of the biggest mysteries of our solar system. A new study has proposed the possible existence of a distant world, nicknamed Planet X2 (PX2), which could help explain the unusual movements and orbital patterns of icy objects in the outer reaches of the Solar System. The research, led by University of Southern Queensland Adjunct Associate Professor Patryk Sofia Lykawka, suggests that the hypothetical planet could have a mass around 1.5 to 2 times that of Earth. Although it has not yet been directly observed, computer simulations indicate that its gravitational influence could account for several puzzling features of distant objects beyond Neptune. Long-standing search for undiscovered planet Published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, the study offers a fresh perspective on the long-standing search for an undiscovered planet in the outer Solar System. According to the researchers, Planet X2 could follow a highly elliptical orbit hundreds of times farther from the Sun than Earth. Its estimated orbital semi-major axis could range between 350 and 500 astronomical units (AU), where one astronomical unit represents the average distance between Earth and the Sun. Even at its closest point to the Sun, PX2 would remain at least 200 AU away, placing it far beyond the orbit of Neptune. The proposed world is different from the widely discussed Planet Nine hypothesis, which suggests that a much more massive planet could be responsible for the unusual orbital behaviour of certain objects in the outer Solar System . Beyond Neptune lies a vast region known as the trans-Neptunian region, which contains numerous icy bodies. Many of these objects are part of the Kuiper Belt, a region that broadly extends between 38 and 50 AU from the Sun. University of Southern Queensland (UniSQ) Adjunct Associate Professor Patryk Sofia Lykawka – who is based at Kindai University in Japan – led the research into the possible world, which he and his team nicknamed ‘Planet X2’ (PX2). Proposed planet would have about 1.5 to 2 times Earth’s mass The proposed planet would have about 1.5 to 2 times Earth’s mass and orbit hundreds of times farther from the Sun than our own planet. While PX2 remains hypothetical, the research offers a new way to investigate the Solar System’s distant outskirts – and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s ongoing survey of the sky could help astronomers to test the theory. “Imagine discovering, after decades of mapping our Solar System, that another planet has been hiding from us all this time,” Associate Professor Lykawka said. “If this planet exists, it could change how we understand the history of our Solar System and how its most distant objects came to follow such unusual orbits.” However, astronomers have also discovered distant objects travelling along unusually elongated and highly inclined orbits that are difficult to explain solely through the gravitational influence of the known planets. One particularly intriguing example is Sedna, a distant icy object whose extremely elongated orbit takes it far beyond the planetary region. Scientists believe that the gravitational pull of an undiscovered planet could be influencing the movements of these objects, potentially explaining why some follow such unusual orbital paths. To investigate the possibility, the research team conducted computer simulations covering approximately 4.5 billion years of Solar System evolution. The simulations examined how a distant planet with different masses and orbital characteristics might influence the movements of icy bodies in the outer Solar System. The results suggest that PX2’s gravity could separate certain objects from Neptune’s gravitational influence and push others into unexpectedly tilted or elongated orbits. The proposed model successfully reproduces several unusual orbital patterns observed among distant trans-Neptunian objects. However, researchers acknowledge that some differences remain between the simulations and actual astronomical observations.
