items.descriptionOriginal: A handful of seeds can carry generations of farming knowledge. In Karnataka's Dharwad district, a group of women has been collecting, preserving, and sharing these seeds, helping farmers continue cultivating indigenous crops suited to the region's rainfed conditions. On November 12, 2026, the Bibi Fatima Women's Self-Help Group (SHG) from Teertha village in Kundgol taluk received the Plant Genome Saviour Community Award, along with a cash prize of Rs 10 lakh, a citation, and a memento. The recognition acknowledges the collective's efforts to conserve more than 250 indigenous seed varieties and revive traditional millet-based mixed cropping systems across 30 villages in Dharwad's rainfed farming areas. The initiative began in 2018, when farmer Bibijaan Maulasaab Halemani brought together 14 other women to establish the collective. Its work includes promoting multi-cropping, maintaining community seed banks, and encouraging sustainable agricultural practices. Photograph: (The Hindu) According to Bibijaan, her interest in seed conservation came from her father, who also preserved seeds. Speaking to The New Indian Express in a report published on November 5, 2026, she said, "My father used to conserve seeds, and I too developed an interest and took to seed conservation." She established the SHG and its seed bank in 2018, with the aim of making good-quality indigenous seeds accessible to farmers and encouraging traditional crop cultivation. A seed bank with more than 250 varieties The group's community seed bank preserves a wide range of indigenous crops, including: - Jawari (sorghum) - 70 varieties of finger millet - 25 varieties of little millet - Two varieties of browntop millet - 10 varieties of foxtail millet - 25 varieties of horse gram - 10 varieties of chickpea - 25 varieties of paddy - Three varieties of green gram - Around a dozen oilseed varieties - Several varieties of vegetables These varieties form part of the region's traditional agricultural diversity. The indigenous millet varieties, in particular, are adapted to local agro-climatic conditions and can withstand variations in weather. The collective has also worked to revive millet-based mixed cropping, in which farmers cultivate multiple crops together rather than depending on a single crop. According to the United Nations Development Programme's Equator Initiative, the group now supports more than 5,000 farmers across 30 villages. Its work includes promoting multi-cropping, maintaining community seed banks, and encouraging sustainable agricultural practices. Beyond seed conservation, the collective has expanded into agricultural processing and livelihood activities. It operates a solar-powered millet processing unit, which helps women produce value-added millet products. The initiative also works on livestock rearing, horticulture, and improving household food and nutritional security. Recognition for community-led seed conservation The national award is not the group's first recognition for its work. In August 2025, the United Nations Development Programme announced Bibifathima Swa Sahaya Sangha as one of the 10 winners of the Equator Prize 2025. The award recognised community-led initiatives working on nature-based solutions under the theme 'Nature for Climate Action', with a focus on women's and young people's leadership. According to the UNDP's August 20, 2025 announcement, the collective received recognition for its work combining traditional agricultural knowledge, seed conservation, renewable energy and climate-resilient farming. Each winning initiative was awarded $10,000. The initiative also works on livestock rearing, horticulture, and improving household food and nutritional security. Photograph: (National Commission for Women/Facebook) For the women of Dharwad, their work continues to centre on collecting indigenous seeds, keeping traditional crop varieties in cultivation and helping farming communities access planting material suited to their local conditions. Sources: 'Karnataka: Bibi Fatima group bags award for saving desi seeds' : By Subhash Chandra N S, Published on 5 November 2026 'UNDP Equator Initiative Award' for Bibi Fatima SHG of Teertha village' : By The Hindu Bureau, Published on 9 August 2025

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM There’s a particular feeling that comes with lifting the lid off the holiday storage bin. The tangle of lights, the ornament with the chipped corner, the little ceramic village you’ve set up on the same shelf for as long as you can remember. It’s comforting, and there’s a reason traditions stick around. But somewhere around the third box, the comfort can start to tip into a sort of déjà vu, and you might catch yourself wondering whether it’s time to start over. Before you head to the store, though, try a different idea. The holiday decorations you already own can look surprisingly different with a little rearranging, a few things from outside, and a willingness to break your own habits. Here are six ways to do it, whether you’re decking the halls for Thanksgiving , Christmas, Hanukkah or all of the above. Rethinking where holiday decorations go Give every piece a new home Most of us decorate on autopilot. The wreath goes on the same hook, the nativity scene lands on the same bookshelf, and the whole house ends up looking exactly like it did last year, because it is exactly like last year. This time, pause before you put anything down. Hold each piece and ask where else it could live. That nativity scene might feel brand new on the entryway table, where it’s the first thing people see. If you’re stuck, give yourself a rule: everything that usually goes upstairs goes downstairs this year, and vice versa. Choose one theme and edit to fit it Instead of pulling out every decoration you own, pick a theme and use only what matches. It can be as simple as one color, like all greens, or one motif, like snowflakes or anything that sparkles. Leaving some favorites in the box for a year can make them feel special again when they come back out, and the pieces you do use will look more intentional together. Bringing in natural and handmade touches Decorate with what’s growing outside Your backyard or a neighborhood walk can fill in a lot of gaps at no cost. A handful of pinecones lined along the mantel, or a few bare branches standing tall in a big vase on the kitchen island, adds texture and makes the familiar pieces around them look fresher. Dried citrus is another easy one. Slice oranges or grapefruit thin, dry them in a low oven until they turn translucent, and string them into a garland. Any extra slices make a lovely garnish for a winter drink. Add something your family made Handmade decorations carry a warmth store-bought ones can’t match. You could decide that this is the year the tree only gets ornaments made at the kitchen table, or have everyone in the house paint their own candle for the menorah. The pieces don’t need to be perfect. The slightly lopsided ones tend to become the favorites. Small changes to familiar holiday decor Trade your lights around String lights are easy to move, so let them wander. Bring the indoor lights outside and the outdoor ones in, or take the strand that usually wraps the tree and frame a doorway with it instead. Before anything goes outside, check that it’s rated for outdoor use, since indoor lights left out in the weather can become a fire hazard. Paint, mix and remake If you’re truly tired of a piece, change how it looks. Spray paint a set of old ornaments in a new color, hand-paint plain candles, or combine figures from two or three mismatched nativity sets into one scene. Experimenting is low-risk here. If you end up disliking the result, you were already ready to retire it, and if you love it, you’ve got something that feels new without buying a single thing, which might be the nicest kind of holiday surprise there is. items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ ΟΠΤΙΜΙΣΤΩΝ Οι γυναίκες στην Αγγλία και την Ουαλία που συνελήφθησαν, προειδοποιήθηκαν ή καταδικάστηκαν για τον τερματισμό της εγκυμοσύνης τους δεν φέρουν πλέον αυτά τα αρχεία. Οι αυτόματες αμβλώσεις τέθηκαν σε ισχύ στις 16 Νοεμβρίου και η αστυνομία και τα δικαστήρια πρέπει τώρα να διαγράψουν τις λεπτομέρειες των προηγούμενων καταδίκων, προφυλάξεων, συλλήψεων και ερευνών όπου μπορούν…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Women in England and Wales who were arrested, cautioned or convicted for ending their own pregnancies no longer carry those records. Automatic abortion pardons took effect on November 16, and police and courts must now delete the details of past convictions, cautions, arrests and investigations wherever they can. The women affected don’t need to apply, pay a fee, or contact anyone. The pardons come under Section 242 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026 , passed earlier this year alongside a separate provision that removed women from criminal law for ending their own pregnancies. Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi, who brought forward the decriminalization amendment, says the change will clear the names of more than 100 women who were “unnecessarily harmed” by an “outdated” law. How the abortion pardons work Records deleted, or treated as deleted The pardon applies to abortion offenses relating to a woman’s own pregnancy, including cases where she acted beyond the legal time limits. Where full deletion from police and court systems isn’t possible, records must be marked so they are treated as erased. Alex Davies-Jones, the minister for victims and tackling violence against women and girls , said the pardons had been a priority. “Women do not have to take any direct action themselves, but can find out more information online and contact our dedicated casework team,” she said. What remains illegal The change ends prosecution of women over their own pregnancies, but abortion itself is still regulated. In England and Wales, abortion with an authorized provider is legal up to 24 weeks, with narrow exceptions after that point, such as when the mother’s life is at risk or the baby would be born with a severe disability. Medication taken at home is permitted before 10 weeks. Doctors and anyone else who act outside the Abortion Act 1967 can still face charges. Ending a Victorian law’s reach Nicola Packer’s five-year ordeal The law that the change dismantles dates to 1861, and the cases brought under it in recent years show what it meant in practice. In 2020, during a Covid lockdown, Nicola Packer, then 41, was prescribed abortion medication by phone through the National Health Service. She believed she was a few weeks pregnant. In fact, she was around 26 weeks along. Her friend Helle Tumbridge, speaking to the BBC with Packer’s consent, said she had experienced what’s known as a cryptic pregnancy. “That’s when you don’t have any sign of a pregnancy, no baby bump, no other symptoms,” she said. After a stillbirth, Packer went to the hospital, and staff called the police. “She was arrested. She spent a time in her hospital room recovering with two police officers present, one was a man. She was treated appallingly,” Tumbridge said. It took five years of investigation before a jury unanimously cleared her. “Of course, by that point the damage had been done, and she’ll live with that trauma for the rest of her life,” Tumbridge said. The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists said at the time that her trial showed “just how outdated and harmful” the law was. Reactions to the pardons Providers and advocates Heidi Stewart of the abortion care provider BPAS acknowledged that a pardon has limits. “While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognises the profound harm caused by their criminalisation and represents a meaningful step towards justice,” she said. Opponents of decriminalization Not everyone sees the change that way. Anti-abortion groups opposed both decriminalization and the pardons, arguing that removing criminal penalties, including for abortions late in pregnancy, leaves the unborn without legal protection. John Deighan, CEO of the Society for the Protection of Unborn Children, said in April that the pardons law “disgraces the children who have been needlessly destroyed in the past.” For the women whose records are now being cleared, the practical effect will show up in background checks, job applications, and travel paperwork that no longer carry a conviction or arrest. Antoniazzi and other supporters will be watching how smoothly police and courts carry out the deletions in the months ahead, since the pardon only works if the paperwork follows. items.descriptionOriginal: An evocative shot of a waterfall of fog spilling into the sea in Mallorca, Spain, took the top honor in the Royal Meteorological Society’s 2026 Weather Photographer of the Year competition. Francisco Bailón Rodríguez captured the image during dawn’s first light, the rising sun illuminating the mist. “There’s a fabulous sense of flow in this image,” competition judge Angela Nicholson said in a statement. “The clouds are transformed into a river flowing over the cliffs. Francisco’s choice of exposure has captured the movement of the clouds perfectly below a beautiful sky with subtle color transitions.” Now in its second decade, the competition highlights the beauty and power of weather while raising awareness of the environmental issues that threaten life on Earth — things like heat, fires, and floods. Thirty images were shortlisted from a pool of over 5,500 taken in 13 countries. In addition to Rodríguez’s shot, eight photos were recognized as winners or runners-up across four categories: public vote, mobile, climate, and main. “These breathtaking images showcase the weather and climate in its pure beauty, complexity, and intensity,” said Liz Bentley, chief executive of the Royal Meteorological Society, per SWNS, adding: “Crucially, many of these images also deliver a powerful and urgent message about the global impact of climate change on environments ranging from parched agricultural land to melting ice caps.” The annual competition is free to enter and open to photographers of all ages and abilities, with judges looking for images that combine skill, meteorological observation, and storytelling. Take a look at the other winners and runners-up, with captions courtesy of contest organizers. Public Vote | Winner “Misty Sunrise Over the Long Coc Tea Hills” by Mahmudul Hasan Mahmudul Hasan/RMetS/SWNS “Captured in the delicate light of dawn, this breathtaking photo reveals the rolling tea hills of Long Coc, Vietnam, emerging through layers of mist.” Mobile Category | Winner “A Winter Morning” by Aung Soe Min Aung Soe MinRMetS/SWNS “A calm winter morning reveals Kuthodaw Pagoda rising through the mist and fog. Aung Soe Min captured the sun rays filtering across the landscape, creating a beautiful sunrise that captures the warmth of the weather and the peaceful serenity of this sacred site in Myanmar.” Climate Award | Winner “Fire” by Erfan Samanfar Erfan Samanfar/RMetS/SWNS “From Marvdasht, Iran, in October 2025, Erfan Samanfar captured a striking image of a farmer attempting to protect their land as fire spreads across the landscape.” Main Category | Runner-Up “Sunrise and Morning Glow” by Weilu Chen Weilu ChenRMetS/SWNS “As the sun rose over the Hong Kong Zhuhai-Macao Bridge, the morning sky was transformed into a spectacular display of golden light.” Public Vote | Runner-Up “Triple Strike NYC” by Dan Martland Dan Martland/RMetS/SWNS “Talk about being in the right place at the right time. From Bayonne, New Jersey, Dan Martland captured this spectacular scene overlooking the New York City skyline, as three lightning strikes lit the sky above the city.” Mobile Category | Runner-Up “A Rainbow Over Loch Duck” by Anthony Bird Anthony BirdRMetS/SWNS “Framed by the rolling hills and water below, a magnificent rainbow arches across the landscape of Loch Duck, Scotland. The scene caught Anthony Bird’s eye so quickly that there was barely time to think, as he simply had to ‘run outside the Airbnb’ to capture it.” Climate Award | Runner-Up “Castles in the Wind” by Andres Miraglia Andres Miraglia/RMetS/SWNS “As an iceberg drifted away from the glacier that released it in Antarctica’s Paradise Harbour, Andres Miraglia captured the moment against a pristine sunset.” Main Category | Third Place “A Supercell in the Sandhills of Nebraska” by Laura Hedien Laura Hedien/RMetS/SWNS “While out storm chasing in the Nebraska sandhills, ‘Mother Nature was kind enough to give us a supercell and lightning at night,’ explains Laura Hedien.” This article was originally written by Dean Murray for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets .

items.descriptionOriginal: Being a clear communicator is a powerful social skill . Not only does it build relationships, but it also creates authentic connections. But in high-pressure situations, confident speaking can start to crumble. We’ve all been there, whether it’s talking to your boss or even sitting across from someone on a first date . It’s easy to start rambling and jumbling your words. To prevent this, communication expert Vinh Giang shares a clever 3-2-1 speaking trick that can help anyone slow down and communicate clearly and concisely when it matters most. What is the 3-2-1 speaking trick? According to Giang, it starts with training your brain for moments when you feel put on the spot. “When someone asks you a question and you’re not prepared, what happens? Your brain hits the panic button,” he says in a YouTube video. As you struggle to verbalize your thoughts, you may start to ramble, which Giang notes, can lead to frustration and embarrassment. To avoid feeling flustered, he offers a 3-2-1 framework to keep in mind when speaking off the cuff. “Without a communication framework to fall back on, your mind goes blank,” he explains. @askvinh These 5 speaking tips will force you to stop rambling! Most people ramble because they’re thinking out loud instead of thinking first. Here’s how to fix it: 1. Pause after important points Give your audience time to process. Silence creates clarity and makes your message land harder. 2. Finish your sentences Stop starting new thoughts before completing the previous one. This is where most rambling begins. 3. The six-year-old test If you can’t explain your idea simply, you don’t understand it well enough yet. Simplicity is mastery. 4. Lead with your point State your conclusion first, then support it. Most people ramble because they’re building toward the point instead of starting with it. 5. Answer with “the one thing” When asked a question, force yourself to give one clear answer. This framework filters mental clutter into focused responses. ♬ original sound – Vinh Giang – Vinh Giang The 3-2-1 framework consists of 3 steps, 2 types, and 1 thing. Using the example of avocados, he explains how it works: 1 thing “The one thing about avocados that I love is that it’s great on a keto diet,” says Giang. 2 types He switches to “ways” instead of “types,” explaining that there are “two ways to eat avocados: you can smash it up or eat it like a fruit [apple].” 3 steps Finally, he explains that there are three steps to preparing avocados: “First step, cut it in half. Step two, mash it up. Step three, salt, pepper, and lemon.” How to use the 3-2-1 speaking trick Giang shares another example of how to use the 3-2-1 speaking trick, this time using the topic of travel. In a clip from a conference, he invites an audience member to try each part. Her answers show how the method works in a real-life scenario: 1 thing “The one thing about travel is it’s magnificent,” the audience member says. “You can go anywhere you want.” 2 types “The two types of travel are: you can travel regionally and you can travel internationally via a plane,” she says. 3 steps “Three steps to travel is plan it, book it, go!” she shares. Giang congratulates her, noting, “That’s the difference between being prepared with a framework, because now you’re excited to communicate. When you’re not prepared, you’re not excited, you’re scared. You don’t want to communicate.” @askvinh The simple solution to stop rambling… If you want to learn what to say when you’re pausing and thinking, you need to learn how to use communication frameworks. ♬ original sound – Vinh Giang – Vinh Giang How viewers reacted to the trick In the comments, people shared their responses to Giang’s video: “I’m officially smarter than I was five minutes ago.” “For an overthinker, this is gold. Thank you tons.” “I’m 40 and honestly, this hits home. I’ve been in situations at work where I froze or rambled because my brain went blank under pressure. The 3-2-1 framework feels so practical and simple to apply. I actually tried it while watching and it gave me structure instantly. Definitely something I’ll practice more in meetings and daily conversations. Thanks for sharing this tool, Vin!” “Immediately used this in a daily mundane small talk conversation that I’m having with someone, and I realized it’s not that I don’t like small talk because I’m not interested with someone… It’s because I don’t know how to do it. Managed to turn small talk into a chain of small conversations that led to more concrete discussions. Thanks a lot for this tip!” “Yeah. This is a big problem that I have. For years I’ve struggled to communicate properly because my brain goes a thousand miles a minute and my mouth tries to keep up.” Frameworks beat panic every time The beauty of Giang’s 3-2-1 trick isn’t that it makes you sound smarter, it’s that it gives your brain somewhere to go the moment it starts to freeze. Whether you’re fielding a tough question from your boss or trying not to ramble on a first date, having even a loose structure to fall back on is often the difference between confident clarity and an awkward, run-on mess. The next time you feel that panic button hit, try reaching for one thing, two types, three steps, and see where it takes you. This article originally appeared in March. It has been updated. The post Communication expert shares 3-2-1 trick to stop rambling when put on the spot appeared first on Upworthy .

Πολλές διάσημες οπτικές ψευδαισθήσεις έχουν δημιουργηθεί σκόπιμα, από το παράθυρο Ames που φαίνεται να κινείται εμπρός και πίσω όταν στην πραγματικότητα περιστρέφεται 360 μοίρες, μέχρι τη σπειροειδή εικόνα που κάνει το Van…
items.descriptionOriginal: Optical illusions are wild. The way our brains perceive what our eyes see can be way off base, even when we’re sure about what we’re looking at. Plenty of famous optical illusions have been created purposefully, from the Ames window that appears to be moving back and forth when it’s actually rotating 360 degrees, to the spiral image that makes Van Gogh’s “Starry Night” look like it’s moving. But sometimes optical illusions happen by accident . Those ones are even more fun because we know they aren’t a result of someone trying to trick our brains. Our brains do the tricking all by themselves. The popular Massimo account on X shared a photo that appears to be a person and two dogs in the snow. The more you look at it, the more you see just that: two dogs and someone who is presumably their owner. Turn the photo every which way and it’s still the same conclusion. That’s a person and two dogs, right? This is how optical illusions mess with your mind. First you see two dogs and their owner, and then… pic.twitter.com/67tm1UPGQa — Massimo (@Rainmaker1973) January 8, 2024 But there are not two dogs in the photo. There are actually three dogs in this picture. Can you see the third? Full confession time: I didn’t see it at first. Not even when someone explained that the “human” is actually a dog. My brain couldn’t see anything but a person with two legs, dressed all in black, with a furry hat and some kind of furry stole or jacket. My brain definitely did not see a black poodle, which is what the “person” actually is. Here’s the hint you need to see it Are you looking at the photo and trying to see it, totally frustrated? The big hint is that the poodle is looking toward the camera. The “hat” on the “person” is the poodle’s poofy tail, and the “scarf/stole” is the poodle’s head. Once you see it, it’s fairly clear, but for many of us, our brains did not process it until it was explicitly drawn out. This outline helps somewhat: That one took me AGES to see. Owner is is a 3rd dog closer to the camera. The black fur hides the contours. pic.twitter.com/X8OvGfqlBV — Shield Maiden Io (@maidensheildio) January 8, 2024 As one person explained, the black fur hides the contours and shadows, so all our brains take in is the outline, which looks very much like a person facing away from us. The internet’s reactions were priceless People’s reactions to the optical illusion were hilarious. One person wrote, “10 years later: I still see two dogs and a man.” 10 years later: I still see two dogs and a man — Farhad (@farhadge) January 8, 2024 Another person wrote, “I agree with ChatGPT :)” and shared a screenshot of the popular AI chatbot describing the photo as having a person in the foreground. Even when asked, “Could the ‘person’ be another dog?” ChatGPT said it was possible, but not likely. Ha. I agree with ChatGPT pic.twitter.com/tNalhK3F9Y — Dr. Eli David (@DrEliDavid) January 8, 2024 One reason we love optical illusions is that they remind us just how very human we are. Unlike a machine that takes in and spits out data, our brains perceive and interpret what our senses bring in, a quality that has helped us through our evolution . But the way our brains piece things together isn’t perfect. Even ChatGPT’s response is merely a reflection of our human imperfections at perception being mirrored back at us . They say seeing is believing, but when we interpret what we’re seeing incorrectly, we end up believing things that might not be real. Sure is fun to play with how our brains work, though. Also a good reminder that what we think we see, even with our own eyes, may not be an accurate picture of reality. This article originally appeared two years ago. It has been updated. The post If you see a person and two dogs in this photo, look again. It’s an optical illusion. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Some people enjoy small talk and are naturally good at it. For others, it feels like mental and emotional torture. There are many reasons why people are nervous about entering social situations where they have to make small talk , such as a work event, a party where they don’t know many people, or school. Some people don’t enjoy small talk because they get frustrated talking about seemingly unimportant topics. At the same time, others are shy and afraid they’ll say the wrong thing or run out of topics of conversation . Therapists suggest that people who are unsure what to say should try the FORD method of conversation starters. It’s an acronym that’s an easy way to remember four different topics of conversation that work with just about anyone. A simple framework for any conversation According to Nicole Arzt, M.S., L.M.F.T , at Social Self, the FORD acronym stands for Family, Occupation, Recreation and Dreams. Here are some examples of questions that fall under each category. Family Just about everyone has a family, so it’s a great way to ask someone to share some information about their personal lives without being too forward. Arzt suggests the following questions when making small talk: You can ask people about their parents, kids, siblings, grandparents, cousins, aunts and uncles, or just family in general. Photo credit: Canva Do you have any siblings? How did you two meet? (if you are meeting a couple for the first time) How old is your child? How is your____ (sister, brother, mother, etc.) doing since ____ (event that happened?) Occupation Just like family, almost everyone has a job. Or, if they do not, that can be an interesting topic as well. Here are some starter questions you can ask someone about their job. What do you do for a living? How do you like working at _____? What’s your favorite part of your job? What made you interested in becoming a _____? Recreation You can learn a lot about a person after knowing how they spend their free time. It’s also an excellent way to determine if someone is like-minded and shares the same interests. Here are some questions to get the ball rolling. It is fun to talk about, well…fun. Photo credit: Canva What do you like to do for fun? Have you watched (or read) ______(popular show/book)? What are you up to this weekend? Dreams Learning someone’s hopes for the future can tell you a lot about who they are on a deeper level. They may have just told you about their current job or how they spend their time. But, ultimately, what do they wish to do with their lives? Here’s how to ask someone about their dreams. Everyone has hopes and dreams. Photo credit: Canva Where do you hope to be working in the next few years? Where would you like to travel? What’s something you’d like to try in the future? Would you ever consider trying _____ (particular hobby or activity)? Don’t just ask questions, share your own answers Arzt also notes that you shouldn’t just be an interviewer. You have to talk about yourself, too. In other words, you need a mutual give-and-take. “Pay attention to someone else’s answers and think about how you can draw from your own experience to connect,” she wrote . When you’re feeling socially anxious , it can be hard to listen to the other person while also thinking about your own responses, so thinking of the FORD acronym for yourself and having something to share in each category ahead of time can be a way to avoid the dreaded awkward silence that sometimes happens during small talk. The right way to balance a conversation It can also be tricky to know how much you should be talking vs. how much you should be listening. If you’re not sure how much to say during a conversation, follow the 43:57 rule . Chris Orlob, then senior director of product marketing at Gong.io, found the 43:57 ratio in a 2016 analysis of sales calls , and Gong’s 2025 update looked at 326,000 calls. Sales success peaked when the salesperson talked 43% of the time and listened for 57%. Even though this insight is from business calls, it applies to everyday social interactions. It’s really about listening and making the other person feel special. After all, who doesn’t love feeling heard and appreciated? Small talk doesn’t have to be torturous, even if it’s something you don’t look forward to. With a little preparation and some genuine curiosity, it might even become enjoyable as you make new connections with people. This article originally appeared three years ago. It has been updated. The post If you struggle with small talk, a simple acronym can make it a lot less painful appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: When you live in a hot, desert city that only gets 11 inches of rainfall per year, water is a precious resource. And yet, laws in Tucson, Arizona , long impeded people’s ability to utilize rainwater efficiently. That is, until Brad Lancaster took a handsaw to his curb and showed the city the result. In 1998 , Lancaster sawed through the curb in front of his house in six places, creating channels to divert rainwater into the space between the street and the sidewalk. Cutting into the curb was illegal, but city officials remained unaware of it for three years, until Lancaster himself told them what he’d done. The transformation was simply too remarkable to keep to himself. Watch: Simple rainwater diversion creates edible oases Lancaster shared with permaculture expert Andrew Millison how channeling rainwater wisely creates a thriving landscape, providing both cooling shade and food for the public. Instead of sending it down concrete curb edges and into storm drains, cuts in the curb move water toward native trees and plants. As Millison says, this simple change is key to “turning depleted neighborhoods into thriving ecosystems.” Lancaster showed Millison how the landscape in his neighborhood has evolved since his initial curb cuts nearly 30 years ago. Not only has he created an impressive rainwater harvesting system on his property, but he’s helped transform the public land adjacent to it as well. A series of streetside basins capture and successively channel rainwater. Each basin holds plant life, much of which is native and edible. It may not look like a traditional orchard, but the trees have edible flowers, cactuses produce fruit, plants produce edible seeds to toss in a salad, and more. “This is the neighborhood rain-irrigated food forest street,” Lancaster explains, “where we’re using the street to water the street trees that shade, cool the street, and feed all those living along the street.” An ancient practice made new again Looking at the Sonoran Desert in its natural state, it’s easy to think it’s not really compatible with human life. It’s hard to tell if the plants are actually alive, much of the flora and fauna look like they could kill you, and you find yourself feeling thirsty just looking at the dry, dusty, sun-baked ground. But more than five million people in the U.S. call that desert home, and Indigenous people have lived there since time immemorial. With less than an inch of rainfall on average per month, there isn’t enough rain to provide adequate water for the human population. The city of Tucson gets 90% of its drinking water from underground aquifers and the Colorado River, but that doesn’t mean the rain the city does get doesn’t make a dent in its water needs. Rainwater harvesting is part of what made human settlement possible in Arizona’s Sonoran Desert. Ancestral peoples of that land were experts in canal-building, diverting water from rivers for irrigation. They also built earthworks , landscape features that direct rainwater and capture it in soil for direct use by plants. In Millison’s video, Lancaster shows examples of earthwork basins created in his neighborhood, including one right in the middle of a roundabout intersection. These are not new ideas, but rather ancient practices being implemented in modern desert cities. How Tucson finally changed its laws It may have been illegal at the time, but Lancaster’s guerrilla action helped change city policy. Tucson Water now runs a green stormwater program for harvesting rainwater and growing trees called Storm to Shade . Tucson Water customers can get a rebate of up to $1,900 for qualifying rainwater harvesting systems, plus a small incentive for planting trees. The city also requires all new commercial properties and road construction to incorporate rainwater harvesting. Storm to Shade program manager Blue Baldwin gives Lancaster credit where it’s due. “The Storm to Shade program truly is the city’s adoption and institutionalization and elevation of all of the pioneering work that Brad did over years and years, below the radar but then bringing it to the city,” she says in Millison’s video. “Brad has been cutting curbs for a very long time,” she adds. “He did it so well with the technology he had available to him. And now we have standard details and construction documents that actually tell construction contractors exactly how to cut a curb.” Who’d have imagined one man’s renegade water diversion would change a whole city’s laws and landscape? You can learn more about rainwater harvesting methods on Lancaster’s website, harvestingrainwater.com , and follow Andrew Millison on YouTube for more amazing permaculture transformations. This article originally appeared in July. It has been updated. The post In 1998, a man illegally cut holes in a Tucson street curb. The result changed the law. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: Gen X teens in 1986 predicted what life would be like today. Here’s what they got right.
items.description: Μπορούν τα παιδιά να προβλέψουν το μέλλον; Το 1966, το Tomorrow’s World του BBC ζήτησε από μια ομάδα 13χρονων να μοιραστούν τις προβλέψεις τους σχετικά με το πώς θα ήταν η ζωή το 2000. Όπως θα περίμενε κανείς, ήταν συναρπαστικό. Δύο δεκαετίες αργότερα, οι showrunner έκαναν ξανά το ίδιο. Μόνο που αυτή τη φορά ρώτησαν τους νεαρούς έφηβους του 1986 τι σκέφτονται τη ζωή σε 2…
items.descriptionOriginal: Can kids predict the future? In 1966, the BBC’s Tomorrow’s World asked a group of 13-year-olds to share their predictions about what life in the year 2000 would be like. As you might expect, it was fascinating. Two decades later, the showrunners did the same thing again. Only this time, they asked the young teens of 1986 what they thought life in 2020 would be like. How did Gen X’s answers about the future differ from those of their Baby Boomer predecessors? The 1966 cohort’s predictions dealt with space travel, robots, and computers. They were concerned about overpopulation and nuclear war. “That was before the manned moon landings, the microprocessor, strategic arms limitation talks, or test-tube babies,” the feather-haired host shared. “So have the hopes and fears of today’s 13-year-olds changed as they look forward to the year 2020?” What the kids of 1986 predicted The kids from 1986 offered their predictions: “Perhaps brain waves to convert into radio waves, sent to someone else, convert back into brain waves. And it’d be like, what would you call it, like a telepathy thing.” “Well, instead of a channel tunnel, you could have something like a space tunnel, where you could go [from] one planet to the other, like bypasses.” “Obviously, nuclear war worries me, but I don’t think that’ll happen unless they’ve got computers that press the button for them. Because no, I don’t think any human being is capable of actually pressing some button that releases all nuclear arms cuz it just means destruction of the world.” “I don’t think they’ll be living on Mars yet, but I think they’ll still be living around here.” “I think they may, unless they have another planet to go to, just there’ll be loads of tower blocks. Or people will be restricted to a certain amount of kids.” “Probably be computers running the country.” Predicting the future is hard work. In 1983, most people viewed the home computer as a passing fad. Two @MIT professors debated the future of PCs. Michael Dertouzos tried to convince us that the home computer is here to stay, 1983 pic.twitter.com/HieMxHBsYx — Vala Afshar (@ValaAfshar) May 8, 2024 “But when it comes to wars and things like that, nuclear bombs, and then they’re designing these different gases that can kill people within seconds and things like that. I think that aspect of technology should be wiped out completely.” So just how accurate were they? It’s interesting how similar many of the issues were between 1966 and 1986. Some of the worries these kids had are still major concerns four decades later. But how accurate were their predictions of what 2020 would hold? The kid talking about not living on Mars yet was right. One could make an argument that computers do run the country, but not necessarily in the way a 13-year-old in 1986 would have imagined. They had no concept of the internet at that point, which made imagining the reality of 2020 impossible. But the threat of nuclear war and questions about whether a person would ever actually “push the button”? That still feels relevant. “Every thinking person fears nuclear war, and every technological state plans for it. Everyone knows it is madness, and every nation has an excuse.” — Carl Sagan — Don Winslow (@donwinslow) March 8, 2026 What they got wrong about the future However, it’s 2026, and there’s nary a space tunnel in sight, so that one was a bust. It’s wild to remember how we assumed things like flying cars and easy space travel would be common in adulthood. (And yet somehow Google Maps still feels like a miracle every time we use it.) It feels like we’re farther from actual telepathy than we imagined in the ’80s, but who knows? With advancements in nanotechnology and the Wild West of AI, even the near future feels entirely unpredictable. In 1985, Marty McFly asked a philosophical question in Back to the Future : “Since when can weathermen predict the weather, let alone the future?” Thankfully, we’ve drastically improved our ability to predict the weather since then. Predicting the future, however, remains as impossible as it has always been. This article originally appeared in March. It has been updated. The post Gen X teens in 1986 predicted what life would be like today. Here’s what they got right. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: In Assam’s Hatikhuli village, elephants were once feared and chased as they moved through farms, creating conflict between people and wildlife. But a simple idea changed the story: feed, don’t fight. Led by 90-year-old conservationist Pradip Kumar Bhuyan, Binod Dulu Bora, and the local community, Hatikhuli began finding ways for humans and elephants to coexist. Villagers planted food for elephants, mapped their migration routes, and worked to create safer corridors for these gentle giants. Today, over 300 elephants pass through Hatikhuli every year, offering a powerful example of what can happen when communities choose understanding over conflict. This is more than an inspiring conservation story. It’s a reminder that protecting wildlife doesn't always mean keeping humans and animals apart. Sometimes, it means learning how to share the same landscape. items.descriptionOriginal: In the mountain villages of Uttarakhand's Tehri Garhwal district, the amount of drinking water available to families can change dramatically with the seasons. Many households depend on natural springs fed by rainfall and water stored underground. As summer approaches and these springs begin to lose their flow, families are left managing increasingly limited supplies. For residents of Unchaun village in the Kirtinagar block, seasonal water shortages have been a concern. And their experience is shared by several other villages in the region. A 2023–24 annual report by Himmotthan Society documents a similar challenge in Sabli village, also in Tehri Garhwal. A survey conducted in June 2022 found that all 52 households depended on a local spring for drinking water during summer because piped supplies were either unreliable or unavailable. The spring's flow dropped from 30 litres per minute during the monsoon to just five litres per minute in May and June. Over four summer months, the village faced an estimated water deficit of 14 lakh litres. These figures offer a glimpse into how difficult the dry months can be for communities that depend on mountain springs. Now, researchers at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Roorkee have developed a new spring in Unchaun, using scientific research to locate and bring underground water to the surface. According to a Ministry of Education announcement on 2 November 2026, the intervention has increased daily drinking-water availability from approximately 500 litres to 1,000 litres or more during the lean season. The interesting part is how the researchers identified where this water could be found. Where does a Himalayan spring get its water? The intervention is part of IIT Roorkee's project, Rejuvenation of Drying Springs in Takoli Gad Catchment of Tehri District, Uttarakhand . Led by Professor Abhayanand Singh Maurya from the Department of Earth Sciences, the project draws on two studies examining how Himalayan springs are replenished and how water moves through underground rock formations. The research was conducted in the Takoli Gad watershed, a 143-square-kilometre area in the Lesser Himalayas, within the Alaknanda River basin. The first study, published in the Hydrological Sciences Journal in October 2026, examined where spring water comes from and how it travels underground. Researchers studied rainfall patterns and used measurements of different forms of hydrogen and oxygen, including radioactive tritium, to trace the movement and replenishment of groundwater. Their findings revealed just how important the monsoon is for sustaining Himalayan springs. Approximately 82% of spring-water recharge in the studied watershed comes from monsoon rainfall. Winter precipitation contributes around 10%, while pre-monsoon rainfall accounts for the remaining 8%. In simpler terms, much of the water that eventually emerges from these springs enters the ground during the rainy season. Some of it remains stored underground, helping sustain water sources even months after the monsoon has ended. The researchers also examined how long water stays underground before emerging through springs. A second study, published in Applied Geochemistry in 2026, looked at how the rocks beneath the hills influence the chemical composition of spring water. It found that interactions between water and carbonate rocks play an important role, alongside seasonal rainfall, soil carbon dioxide and human activities. Together, these studies helped researchers understand how springs are replenished, what influences their water quality and where groundwater might be available. IIT Roorkee Research Doubles Water Availability in a Himalayan Village During Lean Season Turning scientific research into tangible impact, IIT Roorkee has developed a new spring in Unchaun village, Tehri Garhwal, Uttarakhand, increasing lean-season drinking-water availability from approximately 500 litres to 1,000 litres or more per day. Led by Prof. Abhayanand Singh Maurya, Department of Earth Sciences, the initiative combines scientific understanding of spring-recharge dynamics, groundwater processes and geophysical investigations with targeted recharge interventions to address seasonal water scarcity. Supported by Namami Gange, National Mission for Clean Ganga, Ministry of Jal Shakti, Government of India, the project demonstrates the potential of research-driven solutions to strengthen rural water security. Building on two research studies published in Hydrological Sciences Journal and Applied Geochemistry, the initiative highlights how scientific insights can translate into effective, locally relevant interventions for Himalayan communities. With Prof. K. K. Pant, Director, IIT Roorkee, emphasising research with societal impact, this effort reinforces the Institute's commitment to advancing sustainable solutions for critical environmental and water challenges. #IITRoorkee #WaterSecurity #HimalayanWater #NamamiGange #SpringRejuvenation #GroundwaterRecharge #ResearchForImpact #SustainableDevelopment @iitroorkee @Director_IITR @cleanganganmcg @DoWRRDGR_MoJS — IIT Roorkee (@iitroorkee) November 2, 2026 How the team brought underground water to the surface The researchers began by studying the rock formations beneath the hillside to identify areas capable of holding and carrying groundwater. Once they located promising water-bearing layers, they estimated their depth and extent. The team then designed trenches along the uphill slope. These trenches help slow rainwater flowing downhill, allowing more of it to seep into the soil and replenish underground water reserves. At a suitable water-bearing layer, the researchers created a controlled opening that allowed groundwater to emerge at the surface. This resulted in a new spring near the road leading to Chandrabadni Temple. The reported result is an increase of at least 500 litres of drinking water available daily during the lean season, a potentially important improvement for households that depend on local sources. Springs are among the most important sources of freshwater for communities across the Indian Himalayan region. Photograph: (Representational image-Jeremy Graham / Alamy) Could this help other Himalayan villages? Across the Himalayas, springs are an important source of drinking water, particularly in remote villages where other supplies can be unreliable. The Unchaun project offers one way of addressing seasonal shortages: studying how water moves beneath a particular hillside before deciding where to intervene. As Professor Maurya explained in the Ministry of Education release, "Understanding the source, movement and seasonal behaviour of spring water is essential to addressing water scarcity." The project has shown promising early results, but its long-term success will depend on whether the new spring continues to provide water through changing seasons. Researchers will need to monitor its flow and water quality over time. For now, the intervention offers a potentially useful approach for other Himalayan villages facing similar shortages, while showing how research into something as familiar as rainwater can help address everyday water needs. Περίπου 25 δέντρα άντεξαν βαριά και η συγκομιδή δεν περίμενε τους αγοραστές. Για τον Kalaiselvi, έναν πρώην επαγγελματία λογισμικού που είχε περάσει σχεδόν μια δεκαετία εργαζόμενος στις Ηνωμένες Πολιτείες, το πλεόνασμα παρουσίαζε…
items.descriptionOriginal: By the time the amla ripened at her father's farm in Iduvai, Tamil Nadu, there was more fruit than the family could consume or sell fresh. Around 25 trees were bearing heavily, and the harvest would not wait for buyers. For Kalaiselvi, a former software professional who had spent nearly a decade working in the United States, the surplus presented a question: Could the fruit be preserved and sold long after its season had passed? That question led to Aruvi Eco Organics, which now makes more than 25 products, from amla jaggery candy and dried fruit to herbal teas and leaf powders. Kalaiselvi estimates that processing helps the farm use nearly 60 percent of its suitable surplus produce, depending on the season. The venture also supports a six-member core team. "My father laid the foundation for our venture through his commitment to organic farming. My contribution has been to build on that legacy by trying out how we can process the produce, reduce avoidable losses, and make natural food products available to more people," she tells The Better India . A return to her father's farm Kalaiselvi grew up in an agricultural family in Iduvai. In 1999, her father, Subramaniam, began developing their ancestral land into what the family called Aruvi Farm, growing amla, sapota, mango and guava without chemical pesticides. Kalaiselvi estimates that processing helps the farm use nearly 60 percent of its suitable surplus produce, depending on the season. She remembers planting seeds during childhood summer holidays at her aunt's house. Her parents encouraged their daughters to study while keeping a connection to the land, but her own ambitions took her towards computers. After studying computer science and engineering at Kongu Engineering College, she worked in Chennai before moving to the US in 2006 to join her husband. Her IT career included stints at AT&T, Frontier Communications, Verizon and Highmark in Pittsburgh, where she worked as an application developer. In March 2015, the couple returned to India with their two young children. Her father-in-law was facing serious health issues, and they wanted to be closer to their parents and raise their children here. They settled in Chennai, where Kalaiselvi spent time helping the children adjust, then worked in recruitment and scientific publishing. She also started Kana Bags, an initiative making cloth bags as alternatives to plastic ones. When the pandemic disrupted that venture in 2020, with the children's classes moving online, the family began spending more time on the farm in Iduvai. Kalaiselvi saw firsthand the labour behind her father's harvest, and the problem that accompanied it. "I got a closer understanding of the effort behind cultivation and the challenges that come with storing and managing the harvest," she recalls. The amla crop was particularly abundant. Even with buyers, fresh fruit had a limited window in which it could be sold. "Instead of looking at the surplus just as produce that could not be sold in time, I started seeing it as an opportunity to create value-added products," she says. From a dryer in the living room to a food business Her father showed her a newspaper article on value addition, and she joined an online session offered by Tamil Nadu Agricultural University. Sasikumar's connection with the farm goes back further. He joined as a helper in January 2008 and gradually learnt planting, tractor operation, and electrical repairs. She began experimenting with drying amla and sapota, initially using a coir-tray dryer that cost about Rs 28,000. She installed it in her Chennai living room; her father sent fruit from the farm by overnight parcel twice a week. The early batches taught her that turning fruit into a product was more complicated than finding a recipe. She sought training at the ICAR-Krishi Vigyan Kendra in Tirupur, Tamil Nadu Agricultural University in Coimbatore and the National Institute of Food Technology Entrepreneurship and Management. Over roughly two years, she learnt about handling produce, moisture, food safety, packaging and shelf life. Guidance from a food technologist at the Krishi Vigyan Kendra also helped her understand which ideas could be made consistently and sold commercially. "A recipe may work once, but achieving the same taste, texture, and quality consistently across batches is a completely different challenge," she says. "I had to experiment repeatedly, understand how ingredients behave during processing, and learn how factors such as drying, moisture, and storage affect the final product." Training introduced her to around 25 possible products. Rather than produce everything, she and her father chose ideas that suited what grew on the farm and their preference for avoiding artificial colours, flavours and synthetic preservatives. In 2021, the family also tested selling sapota and mango directly to consumers . Their first order was for sapota, but the pilot reinforced how difficult it could be to find buyers before fruit spoiled. By April 2022, the family had moved permanently to Iduvai. Working alongside Subramaniam, Kalaiselvi made the experiments more systematic, and Aruvi began commercial sales towards the end of that year. A June 2023 video about her journey on the agricultural YouTube channel Tamizhan Agri helped introduce the products to a wider audience. What goes into making 25+ natural food products Aruvi's catalogue has grown to more than 25 products, including over a dozen made with amla. Alongside jaggery-sweetened amla candy are dried mango and sapota, moringa and curry leaf powders, herbal infusions and products made from jamun seeds. "I never set out to build a large product line. Each new addition came from identifying an opportunity to make better use of what we grew and finding ways to meet customer needs," Kalaiselvi says. Over roughly two years, she learnt about handling produce, moisture, food safety, packaging and shelf life. The choices extend to packaging. Aruvi uses cotton bags for its herbal dip teas instead of nylon mesh. Produce is harvested, sorted and cleaned, with damaged portions removed. Depending on the product, the team cuts or deseeds fruit before drying or further processing. The team checks each batch for appearance, texture, aroma and moisture, then packages and stores it carefully. Samples are sent to a NABL-accredited laboratory at Tamil Nadu Agricultural University in Coimbatore for nutritional and quality assessment. Working without synthetic preservatives makes consistent processing and storage especially important. The family farm supplies most ingredients, with additional produce sourced from farmers and producers around Tirupur when needed. For Kalaiselvi, this is where her previous career has proved useful. The discipline of software development, she says, helped her approach new recipes through testing, documentation and problem-solving, even as she learnt the practicalities of working with seasonal crops. The people behind every packet As orders grew, Aruvi's work created roles beyond the family. Six people now make up its core team across farming, processing, packaging and operations. For some, the change has meant a dependable income; for others, a chance to use or develop new skills. Mahalakshmi, 41, joined in February 2024 after spotting a banner advertising work at the farm gate. A single mother raising two children, she had previously worked in tailoring and papad-making units. She began by collecting leaves and fruit, then learnt food processing from Kalaiselvi. Today she helps maintain the workspace, stitches cotton tea bags and operates the amla-deseeding machine. "I did not have much knowledge of food processing or how farm produce could be turned into different products," she says. "At Aruvi Eco, I got the opportunity to learn new skills under the guidance of Kalaiselvi ma'am." Earning Rs 5,000 a week has made a difference at home. Her daughter is in college and her teenage son is studying for a diploma. Where she once sometimes turned to relatives for help with education expenses, she says she can now meet more of those costs herself. "Today, I feel proud that I can earn and take care of many of my family's needs myself," she says. "Apart from being my only source of income, this job is an opportunity to build a better future for my children." Ramar and his wife Uma joined in March 2026. They had moved to Tirupur in search of work and were employed at a stitching unit when they saw an advertisement for jobs at Aruvi. Ramar has a degree in agriculture and now handles planting, watering, pruning and tree care under Subramaniam's guidance. Uma works with fruit and flowers in processing. He earns Rs 6,000 a week and she earns Rs 4,000. Together, they support three children and their elderly parents. The family farm supplies most ingredients, with additional produce sourced from farmers and producers around Tirupur when needed. "I was happy to get an opportunity to return to agriculture, while my wife could contribute to food processing," Ramar says. Sasikumar's connection with the farm goes back further . He joined as a helper in January 2008 and gradually learnt planting, tractor operation, maintenance, plumbing and electrical repairs. Today he manages much of the daily farm work and coordinates packing and dispatch. His wife, Sumithra, stitches cotton tea bags from home using a machine supplied by Kalaiselvi. When a customer complained that a tea bag floated instead of staying immersed, Sasikumar suggested adding two stitches. The adjustment worked and became part of the process. "I never imagined that a job I started as a helper would allow me to learn so many skills and take on such responsibilities," he says. "I feel that my experience matters and that I can contribute ideas that make a real difference to the business." A longer life for the fruit, and a new beginning after 40 Kalaiselvi estimates that nearly 60 percent of suitable surplus produce that might previously have gone unused is now processed. It is an approximate, seasonal figure, rather than a fixed share of everything the farm grows. Processing also means the family has more ways to earn from fruit instead of relying only on fresh-produce prices during a short harvest window. By December 2024, Aruvi had reached more than 4,000 customers and recorded around 450 orders in one month. Sales have come through its website, Amazon and WhatsApp, while exhibitions, farmers' markets and food events have helped people across India discover the products. Some ingredients are sourced from neighbouring producers, giving the business opportunities to connect with other growers too. Kalaiselvi saw firsthand the labour behind her father's harvest, and the problem that accompanied it. Growth comes with its own demands. Availability changes with each season, small batches take planning, and products without synthetic preservatives need careful hygiene and moisture control. Kalaiselvi has had to learn about equipment, investment, pricing and winning customer trust. "Perhaps the biggest challenge was changing our own mindset. From thinking like farmers who wanted to avoid wastage to thinking like entrepreneurs who had to create a product, a brand, and a market around that surplus," she says. She hopes to improve processing capacity and quality checks, work with more local farmers, reach retailers and business customers, and create more jobs. But she keeps returning to the person who made the journey possible: her father, who began tending the ancestral land long before she imagined working on it herself. "Today, the farm means much more to me than a piece of ancestral land. It is a part of my family's history, a teacher, a workplace, and the foundation of Aruvi Eco," she says. She was over 40 when she began learning food processing. Starting again meant being a beginner after years in an established career, a possibility she hopes other women will consider too. Mahalakshmi, 41, joined in February 2024 after spotting a banner advertising work at the farm gate. "I started this journey in a completely new field after 40, and there were many things I had to learn from scratch," she says. "That experience has given me a strong belief that women, and anyone who feels it is 'too late' to begin something new, should not let age stop them." What began as a question about unsold amla has become a way to carry forward her father's work, give the harvest more time to find a buyer and build livelihoods around the farm she once visited on holidays. All pictures courtesy Kalaiselvi.

items.title: Η ανακάλυψη του Αλτσχάιμερ αποκαλύπτει ένα κρυφό ελάττωμα στο σύστημα καθαρισμού του εγκεφάλου
items.titleOriginal: Alzheimer’s breakthrough exposes a hidden flaw in the brain’s cleanup system
items.description: Οι επιστήμονες εντόπισαν ένα γονίδιο που βοηθά τα κύτταρα του ανοσοποιητικού συστήματος του εγκεφάλου να περιέχουν επιβλαβείς πλάκες που συνδέονται με τη νόσο του Αλτσχάιμερ, αποκαλύπτοντας πιθανώς έναν νέο τρόπο καταπολέμησης της νόσου. Όταν το γονίδιο δυσλειτουργούσε στα ποντίκια, η τοξική συσσώρευση επιταχύνθηκε και οι γνωστικές ικανότητες μειώθηκαν, δημιουργώντας ελπίδες ότι η αποκατάσταση της λειτουργίας του θα μπορούσε να βοηθήσει στην προστασία του εγκεφάλου.
items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have identified a gene that helps the brain’s immune cells contain harmful plaques linked to Alzheimer’s, potentially revealing a new way to fight the disease. When the gene malfunctioned in mice, toxic buildup accelerated and cognitive abilities declined, raising hopes that restoring its function could help protect the brain.

items.descriptionOriginal: A family in Los Angeles’ Lake Balboa neighborhood has a holiday tradition that dates back about 80 years. Every Thanksgiving, the host and a helper write “Turkey Notes” for all the loved ones attending the feast. The only rule? Include the word “turkey” somewhere in the text. The notes range from silly rhymes (“Turkey red, turkey yellow, turkey says you’re an awesome fellow”) to sincere celebrations of guests’ recent accomplishments. The writers then wrap the notes in colorful tissue paper and “roll them like a Tootsie Roll with ribbon on each end,” Nice News reader Sadie shared, adding that the ritual makes for some of her favorite memories. Sadie is one of the dozens of readers who answered our call earlier this month to submit the seasonal family traditions they partake in. Multiple made us laugh out loud, while others were deeply touching. We rounded up a selection for you to peruse — and they just might inspire new shared activities for your own holiday gatherings. Iuliia Anisimova—iStock/Getty Images Plus The hood ornament from my husband’s mother’s car he wrecked as a teenager. It was his only Christmas gift that year. It’s the first ornament we hang every year. – Katherine (Lake Wylie, South Carolina) Thanksgiving Eve, we have a family/friend gathering called BAGG, which stands for Bucket-A-Go-Go. We started this tradition because my husband was tired of eating turkey on Thanksgiving and wanted a change. Nobody wanted to change the Thanksgiving menu, so BAGG was created! Every family brings their own meal but the No. 1 rule is that it must NOT be turkey! The tradition started with a bucket of chicken but now it is whatever the family brings (but NO turkey). One year someone brought a turkey sandwich and they were booed! – Lauren (Roanoke, Virginia) Cookies! We have a cookie trade! Everyone bakes two to three different types of cookies and then we get together for a Christmas party and eat cookies while spending time together. At the end of the get-together, we all split up the cookies so everyone gets to take home a few of each type of cookie. – Stacy (La Mesa, California) My three children were young when their dad and I divorced. He lived in a different state and this meant the children were always torn between celebrating Thanksgiving and Christmas with either mom or dad. So the children and I invited our exclusive holiday — Thanksmas — which was celebrated in early December. We decorated with both fall and Christmas decorations, cooked a meal of Thanksgiving and Christmas dishes, and enjoyed holiday music. And they never had to decide between celebrating Thanksmas with mom or dad each year — it was ours, and ours alone! – Norine (Winchester, Virginia) In our family, we write funny clues on the gifts. While opening them, we read the clues aloud and try to guess what the gift is. – Jennifer (Duluth, Minnesota) My brother sent me an orange tree the year our dad died. Purple and orange were his favorite colors, so I decorated it with purple ornaments. It now goes up in October and transitions from a Halloween tree with bats to a Thanksgiving tree with turkey hands made by my 10 grandchildren, and then to the Christmas tree. Reminders of both my dad and my thoughtful brother. – Debra (Olathe, Kansas) I love putting out my holiday decorations from my favorite holidays, Diwali and Thanksgiving to Christmas. I also celebrate my decorations every year inside my house trying new styles as I desire after talking with my household for what we all like most. – Sautam (Massachusetts) Every year my husband and I host “Nacho Christmas.” It came about because we both wanted a chill holiday with plenty of quality time with any friends and family that want to stop through. We set up the nacho bar so people can eat whenever they come by — no need to coordinate a meal at a set time. … It’s such a huge hit that a friend had a terrible nightmare where I told her she can’t come anymore and she woke up crying. Nacho Christmas for the win. – Wendy (Chicago, Illinois) My son and I watch a holiday movie every night, beginning with Miracle on 34th Street on Thanksgiving Eve. We will have the tree up and lit as well, and then add a few ornaments every day. We always save a few so friends and family can hang something when they come over. Of course we go to see the tree at Rockefeller Center and the Rockettes every year as well! – Peggy (New York City) Making Aebleskivers, a Danish round ball pancake, on Christmas morning. They are the size of a golf ball and you make them in a pan with round holes. When the bottom of the pancake is cooked, you turn it over to cook the top side using a knitting needle. When done they can be eaten as is or with powdered sugar or honey, or you can split them open and add jam, whipped cream, or pudding in the middle. It has been a family tradition for 100 years. – Kathy (Texas) Butterscotch Schnapps milkshakes. Ice cream, milk, and Schnapps. That’s it. Sit around, talk, and drink. It’s fantastic. – Emery (Saskatchewan, Canada) My family (me, my husband Tim, and our two sons: TJ, 22, and Joey, 18) saves all the holiday cards we receive throughout the season and open them all at once after dessert on Christmas Eve. We started this tradition about 10 years ago and it’s been a favorite of everyone’s. This way, Tim and I can share who our nonlocal friends are, but over time, our sons know them and recognize them, even if they’ve never met them in person. And it’s a good way for someone not to miss some important updates. We just wish more friends and families still sent out cards. We love them. – Amy (Poulsbo, Washington) Every year for Hanukkah when my kids were still at home, we made latkes, played games, lit candles, and invited friends over. Some years, instead of giving individual gifts, we did one big family experience together. When the kids were in their teens, we decided that the first of the eight nights would be dedicated to charity, so instead of exchanging presents, we bought them for others in need or made a donation. – Elaine (Baltimore, Maryland) While raising our children in New Hampshire, we had many winter days where we lost electricity because of ice/snow storms. When the kids were very young, we lost electricity one Christmas Eve. But having a wood stove as the primary way to heat the house, at least we were warm. So, for lighting, we placed lit candles in every room and cooked some basic foods on top of the wood stove. It was magical for the children. This started a tradition on every Christmas Eve of turning off all the lights in the house, lighting only candles, and eating just hors d’oeuvres — which we have now done for 30-plus years. – Jim (North Carolina) Every Christmas, I plan a solo trip that I look forward to all year. I try to fly on Christmas Day and bring a little gift (usually a box of chocolates) for the flight attendants. While flying on the holiday tends to be a little less expensive, the real benefit is that people are kinder and more patient with one another. It reminds me of the airport scene at the beginning of Love Actually . – Marie (Frankfurt) My father is a Methodist minister. When he was in seminary shortly after World War II, he attended a Christmas party. A warm punch was served and he really liked it. He obtained the recipe and we’ve made the wassail punch every year since! We still have the original typed recipe on crinkly typewriter paper. – Carol (Alameda, California) Fruitcakes. Every Halloween weekend, I make fruitcakes with raisins, currants, apricots, pecans, cinnamon, clove, mace, and, yes, some of the traditional citron but less. Sherry and brandy poured over them every weekend until the weeks between Thanksgiving and Christmas. My paternal grandmother kept them in her pantry and I loved to watch her take them out, unwrap the wax paper, and pour sherry through cheesecloth then re-wrap and set on the self. She is with me all the time I make these. – Susan Conklin (Hood River, Oregon) My two sons are grown now, but when they were small they would make an ornament for the tree. The early ones were simple, a scrap of fabric (I had to sew the seams as they were only 2 and 4 years old), stuffed little pillows with fluffy cotton. As the years went by, the ornaments became quite amazing for little hands. As a 4-year-old, my youngest was able to complete a framed cross stitch on his own. This was a tradition until they each left for college. I now hang about 30 wildly creative ornaments on my own tree. – Ki’ihele (Hawai’i) Making gifts for my family and my friends, be it knitted mittens, a painting, or special desserts, while I enjoy the winter scenery outside my kitchen window. – Dianne (River Falls, Wisconsin) About a decade ago, I began a tradition with my son (now 13) that we call the thankful tree. I found a little decorative tree and we have leaf-shaped papers with string. Every night of November, we each write down something we are grateful for from that day, share them out loud, and hang them on the tree. By the end of the month, our tree (and hearts) are bursting with gratitude, and I save and label the “leaves” from each year, so we can look back on memories and gratitude. – Sarah (Denver, Colorado) I am one of 10 children. When we were born, my mother knit us a Christmas stocking with our names on it. As we married and had children, she knit stockings for our spouses and her grandchildren. My brother-in-law built a faux fireplace that we keep at the Elks Club. We get together every Christmas Eve and hang our stockings! There are usually 40-50 stockings! – Mary (Warren, New Jersey) Every December, we delight in attending a carol service at a huge old church on Bloor St. — a main street in the downtown. People put twenties on the collection plate which goes entirely to support the Toronto Star Santa Claus Fund begun by newspaper editor Joe Atkinson so underprivileged children would receive a Christmas gift. Boxes contain mitts, warm hats, books, candy, etc. This was especially welcomed during the Great Depression and continues the spirit of giving to this day! – Gail (Toronto, Canada) Since college, my sibling and I have played Santa for our parents. It’s our way of giving back. Yes, our parents still play Santa for us, and Santa gifts are, dare I say, now more anticipated than family gifts. – Eli (Seattle, Washington) Every year, we rent a big house or conference center for around 20 family members. We bring a Ping-Pong table if need be and we play card games, board games, puzzles, and, of course, Ping-Pong. Wednesday night is cheese streak night. On Thursday, we all work to make the Thanksgiving meal. Friday we hike and play, play, play. It never gets old. This year we are trying a new location, the Jersey Shore. – Joyce (Ottsville, Pennsylvania) My grandmother’s favorite color was purple; she passed about 20 years ago. Each year for Christmas, my mom and I wrap a special package in purple paper to give to each other from my grandmom, Mabelle. – Kimberleigh (Maryland) RELATED: We Asked Readers to Share the Best Compliments They’ve Received

items.title: Το 1992, η Annie Lennox διέλυσε τον David Bowie ενώ έκανε πρόβα το "Under Pressure" για το αφιέρωμα του Freddie Mercury.
items.titleOriginal: In 1992, Annie Lennox blew David Bowie away while rehearsing ‘Under Pressure’ for Freddie Mercury tribute
items.description: Οι θαυμαστές της ροκ σε όλο τον κόσμο ήταν ακόμα σε πένθος. Μόλις πέντε μήνες μετά τον θάνατο του frontman των Queen, Freddie Mercury, οι σύντροφοί του συγκέντρωσαν μερικά από τα μεγαλύτερα ονόματα της μουσικής για μια συναυλία στο Wembley Stadium του Λονδίνου. Δεν έμοιαζε με τίποτα από το Live Aid. Η συναυλία αφιερώματος του Freddie Mercury ξεκίνησε ως αποχαιρετιστήριο σε ένα από τα σπουδαιότερα τραγούδια της ροκ…
items.descriptionOriginal: Rock fans around the world were still in mourning. A mere five months after the death of Queen frontman Freddie Mercury, his bandmates gathered some of the biggest names in music for a concert at London’s Wembley Stadium. It was unlike anything since Live Aid . The Freddie Mercury Tribute Concert began as a fond farewell to one of rock’s greatest legends . Over the course of the night, it became a global call for compassion and action in the fight against HIV/AIDS. Photo credit: “ Freddie Mercury ” by kentarotakizawa is licensed under CC BY 2.0 . – Fans are thrilled to hear Freddie Mercury's iconic voice once again. Globally, the concert reached an estimated audience of about a billion people. Onstage, rock stars from Metallica and Elton John to George Michael and Guns N’ Roses paid homage to Mercury and the songs he crafted with Queen. When David Bowie stepped onstage to perform “Under Pressure,” the audience knew something special was about to happen. What they did not know was who would take on the challenge of performing Mercury’s half of the song. A rehearsal that revealed something extraordinary In 1981, “Under Pressure” reached the #1 spot on the singles charts in over 10 countries. It was Queen’s second-ever #1 single in the UK, and, for Bowie, his third UK #1 at that point. Mercury’s vocals carry enormous emotional weight and replacing him was understandably intimidating. Enter an unexpected choice: former Eurythmics lead singer Annie Lennox. In rehearsal footage that has circulated online for years, you can see for yourself just how nervous everyone looks as surviving Queen bandmates Brian May, John Deacon, and Roger Taylor start to work through the song. David Bowie can be seen chain-smoking throughout. Lennox, known for her controlled vocals in hits like “Sweet Dreams (Are Made of These),” is searching for the right balance between honoring the original and making it her own. Just to add to the pressure, there was only time for a single rehearsal on the soundstage at Bray Studios before the big Wembley Stadium show. The moment when the vibes completely shift At first, Lennox appears genuinely nervous. Her attempt at Mercury’s opening jazz scat feels tentative. It’s when she reaches the song’s soaring “Why can’t we give love?” section that the room’s temperature changes. Bowie visibly lights up, his confidence growing. Brian May cracks a smile in between power chords. Everyone seems to realize the same thing at the same moment: this is going to work. And if you watch closely, you can spot another future showstopper in the background: George Michael. George Michael, singing along with Queen, David Bowie, and Annie Lennox to ‘Under Pressure’ (Media Credit: YouTube ) Michael was waiting in the wings to rehearse his own tribute version of “Somebody to Love,” a performance many still consider one of the greatest live Queen tributes ever. In this candid moment, however, he’s just a fan captivated by Bowie and Lennox’s performances as they ready themselves to perform “Under Pressure” in front of 76,000 screaming fans. An iconic performance that brings the house down The one-night-only live performance was every bit as dramatic as it was transformative. Lennox wore a gown by Antony Price, a designer Bowie suggested. In a 2025 interview with CBS Mornings , Lennox shared she initially had “sticker shock” at the high price point, but she trusted Bowie’s well-honed presentational instincts. At the last minute, she added some final dramatic flair: harlequinesque makeup. And the surprises kept coming. The most thrilling part of the performance happened entirely on the fly. During the song’s climax, Lennox spontaneously reached out, wrapped her arm tightly around Bowie’s neck, and pulled him in close. In the same CBS Mornings interview, Lennox laughed about how risky it felt at the time: “We didn’t plan that…I’m looking at him out of the side of my eye and he just stood there. He knew exactly what to do because he was so consummate. He just let me kind of slither around…Can you imagine if it hadn’t worked? A lot of egg on my face.” As stunning as the concert footage is, the rehearsal remains the more revealing document. This fly-on-the-wall footage captures a fleeting moment when a group of world-class artists came together not to chase perfection, but to honor a friend and forever icon. This article originally appeared in June. It has been updated. The post In 1992, Annie Lennox blew David Bowie away while rehearsing ‘Under Pressure’ for Freddie Mercury tribute appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: 4 καθημερινές φράσεις που μπορεί να υποδηλώνουν ότι κάποιος είναι ιδιαίτερα ευφυής

items.description: Τόσο συχνά, εξισώνουμε τη νοημοσύνη με τυποποιημένες δοκιμές, πτυχία ή κατάταξη σε μια τάξη αποφοίτησης. Το άτομο που έχει GPA 4,0 και υψηλό σκορ SAT είναι μάλλον πολύ έξυπνο.
