items.descriptionOriginal: At a school in Ammaiyappan, Thiruvarur district, a discarded newspaper found a new purpose. Instead of being thrown away, it was folded into a waste bag, fitted with jute handles and coated with melted crayons to make it resistant to moisture. The idea was to offer households an alternative to polythene bags while addressing another problem: the difficulty of managing mixed waste. The students behind the initiative, called Decom POSSIBLE, have now won the 'Build a Waste-Free World' category at the inaugural I CAN Earthshot Challenge, earning a $2,000 grant to further develop their work. The project is developed by students of SSATN Panchayat Union Middle School in Ammaiyappan (West), Tamil Nadu. Turning discarded paper into an alternative The bags were made using materials that were readily available to the students. Old newspapers formed the main body, while jute was used for the handles. Discarded crayons were melted and applied as a coating to help the bags withstand moisture. The students took the idea beyond the school premises. Over a period of more than 30 days, they visited households, distributed the bags and spoke to residents about waste segregation. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Earthshot Prize (@earthshotprize) The initiative was designed to address mixed waste disposal as well as the challenges sanitation workers face when handling waste that has not been separated at source. But the students' work did not stop with the bags. A composting pit at school, and a community centre revived At the school, the team established a composting pit measuring 8 feet long, 2 feet wide and 3 feet deep. Organic waste, once separated from other household and school waste, was placed in the pit and converted into manure within a month. This gave the students a way to demonstrate what happens when biodegradable waste is kept separate instead of being mixed with plastic and other discarded mater The initiative also extended to an existing community facility. Within two weeks, the students helped revive a previously inactive community composting centre, creating another avenue for processing organic waste locally. The challenge invited children between nine and 17 years to identify environmental problems in their communities and develop solutions that could be put into practice. Photograph: (Earthshot Prize) The project reports that its activities have benefited 502 people. It also led to a response from the local panchayat: following the initiative, the panchayat announced that waste would have to be separately segregated before collection from 1 October 2026. This local policy change is an important part of the project. Household-level segregation depends not only on residents separating their waste, but also on collection systems that maintain that separation. When wet and dry waste are mixed again during collection, much of the effort made at home can be undone. From a school initiative to a national platform Decom POSSIBLE was among 15 finalist projects selected for the inaugural I CAN Earthshot Challenge. The finalists represented nine Indian states and Delhi, and their projects addressed five environmental priorities: protecting and restoring nature, reviving rivers, lakes and oceans, cleaning the air, building a waste-free world and fixing the climate. The challenge was organised by The Earthshot Prize in partnership with Alana and Design for Change. It invited children between nine and 17 years to identify environmental problems in their communities and develop solutions that could be put into practice. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Earthshot Prize (@earthshotprize) The other winning projects included a low-cost cooling crate developed by students in Punjab to keep vegetables fresh in hot conditions, biodegradable diyas designed to reduce pollution in the Godavari in Maharashtra , and a natural-material air filter developed by students in Bengaluru. For the students in Ammaiyappan, the next step is to keep the practices going beyond the award. According to the project details published by The Earthshot Prize, they plan to encourage more households to adopt composting and take the model to neighbouring schools and panchayats. Their next challenge will be to sustain these practices and encourage more households to adopt them. Sources: 'Discover the Winners of the Inaugural I CAN Earthshot Challenge' : Published on 22 October 2026 'The Earthshot Prize, Alana and Design for Change Announce Finalists of Nationwide I CAN Earthshot Challenge' : By NewsVoir, Published on 23 October 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: Note: The Vyasa Project does not publicly disclose the names of children who contribute to its platform. The child featured in this story has therefore been identified by their chosen nickname. For a Class 5 student (nickname Super_Goalie) at Royal Concorde International School in Bengaluru, narrating a story meant becoming six different people at once. One of the stories the young reader chose was Arjuna and the Bird's Eye from the Mahabharata. Having heard it from their parents several times, the child knew the story well. But recording it for other children offered a new experience: bringing each character to life with a different voice. "I particularly enjoyed this one because I could use different voices for the five Pandavas and their guru, Dronacharya. It felt like I could become six different people all at once," he shares. "I had heard this story from my parents many times, so I already knew it well. But this time, I got to tell it in my own way and add my own style." For the child, it was an opportunity to have fun with a familiar story. But with every page read aloud and every recording made, children are also practising their reading, exploring expression and becoming more comfortable with their own voices. A Class 5 student brings characters from the Mahabharata to life by narrating 'Arjuna and the Bird's Eye' in different voices for other children. This is the idea behind The Vyasa Project, a free, non-profit audio library where children narrate stories for other children. The initiative brings together two simple pleasures: reading a good story and listening to another child tell it. Its founders hope that this experience will encourage more children to pick up books, enjoy reading and discover the confidence that comes with expressing themselves. When children become storytellers The process begins with children exploring a curated collection of stories on the Vyasa Project platform. They can choose from Panchatantra tales, Aesop's fables, folktales, abridged classics and poems. The collection includes stories in English, Hindi, Telugu, Bangla and Kannada and Marathi, allowing children to explore narratives in languages they are comfortable with. From the Panchatantra to Aesop's fables, the platform offers children a growing collection of stories they can read, narrate or simply listen to. Once they have chosen a story, children practise reading it before recording their narration. They can listen to their recordings, re-record them if needed, and submit them for review. Every submission is manually checked before being added to the library. If a recording cannot be published because of quality issues, the child receives detailed feedback to help improve it. The platform also has demonstration videos to help children and parents understand its features and navigate the process. For Karan S Kumar, co-founder of The Vyasa Project, the idea comes from his own childhood relationship with books. "I was the kind of child who always had a book open. Those stories took me to worlds I could never have reached otherwise, and somewhere along the way they shaped how I think, how I speak and how I see other people," he says. He wanted to bring that same sense of wonder to more children. The idea of children narrating stories for their peers became a way to make reading feel less like a lesson and more like a shared experience. "When a child narrates a story, something changes. They find their voice and their confidence, and they discover that what they have to say matters. And when another child listens, it feels less like being taught and more like a friend sharing something special," he adds. A library that grows with every child's voice The stories are selected to be age-appropriate, engaging and enjoyable, with interesting characters, humour, unexpected twists and meaningful themes. Priyanka Tadipatri, co-founder of the project, says the English collection began with stories from different storytelling traditions, including the Panchatantra, Arabian Nights, Grimm's fairy tales, Aesop's fables and Zanzibar tales. It also includes abridged works by authors such as Charles Dickens, Mark Twain, L Frank Baum and Oscar Wilde. Karan S Kumar and Priyanka Tadipatri, co-founders of The Vyasa Project, hope to make reading a shared experience by encouraging children to tell stories to their peers. The collection has since expanded into regional languages, with the founders hoping to add more Indian and international languages over time. Importantly, children do not have to record stories to use the library. They can simply listen to narrations uploaded by other young readers and explore stories across genres and languages. The founders have also deliberately kept the platform free of likes, comments and peer-to-peer messaging. Their intention is to create an experience similar to visiting a library: children come to discover stories, enjoy them and return whenever they want to read or listen again. For Madurai Sridhar, a grandparent whose granddaughter regularly uses the platform, this interest has been particularly encouraging. "My granddaughter asks me to log in to The Vyasa Project regularly. What she loves most isn't the listening; it's reading stories aloud and recording them for other children. We're strict about screen time at home, and this is one of the few things on a screen I'm happy to say yes to," he says. He adds that seeing his granddaughter so absorbed in the activity has been reassuring, especially when children often move quickly from one activity to another. The early response has been encouraging. Within three months of starting the project, the team received close to 700 recordings across languages, with several children contributing more than 10 narrations each. Priyanka says they have also noticed children becoming more comfortable with narration after initially hesitating. Some begin tentatively but grow more confident within just a few paragraphs. A young reader records a story for The Vyasa Project, helping other children discover the joy of reading through listening. "We do not expect children to have perfect pronunciation or error-free submissions. For us, it is more important that they have fun, enjoy the journey and hopefully fall in love with stories and books," she says. Nischala Agnihotri, a working mother and children's author of Yellow Kabbadi , believes the value of reading extends beyond developing language and cognitive skills. "It's not just about cognitive skills. Reading as a habit works at a deeper level. It builds the unseen. It works on their character, personality, and how they develop their first response and thinking patterns," she says. She believes that folklore, poetry and storytelling traditions can play an important role in shaping how children understand the world. For her, The Vyasa Project is helping bring these experiences to more children. Making reading a shared experience To encourage more children to participate, The Vyasa Project is organising Readers' Quest 2026, a seven-day online storytelling challenge during National Library Week, from 14 to 20 November. Open to children in Grades 1 to 7, or those aged 6 to 12, the challenge invites participants to contribute at least seven narrations during the week. Up to 20 winners across junior and senior categories will receive prizes, certificates, and an opportunity to attend a Voice and Storytelling workshop led by RJ Jayashree Raj. But for the founders, the larger idea goes beyond a week-long challenge or the number of recordings in the library. With every story narrated, The Vyasa Project hopes to inspire another child to pick up a book and discover the joy of reading. As Karan puts it, "A child doesn't have to narrate a story to benefit from the platform. Listening is just as central to the experience." And perhaps that is what makes the idea special. One child discovers a story, another finds the courage to narrate it, and someone else listens and feels inspired to pick up a book. With every new voice added to the library, another child gets an invitation to discover a world between the pages. All images courtesy of Priyanka Tadipatri and The Blooming Dale School

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Singapore’s Southern Islands and the Strait of Sicily and Tunisian Plateau Named Mission Blue Hope Spots® Reading Time: 5 minutes From one of the world’s busiest ports to a Mediterranean crossroads, two new Hope Spots show that ocean protection can thrive wherever communities choose to work together. Mission Blue has designated Singapore’s Southern Islands as a new Hope Spot, championed by Friends of Marine Park, recognising an extraordinary tropical marine ecosystem where marine life, science, culture, and one of the world’s busiest waterways converge. The Hope Spot designation celebrates decades of work by Singapore’s marine community, alongside government agencies, scientists, educators, and other partners, to better understand and conserve the country’s marine heritage. One example is the establishment of Sisters’ Islands Marine Park, Singapore’s first marine park, which helps safeguard the rich marine biodiversity and ecosystems of the Southern Islands. More than 250 species of hard coral have been recorded around the Southern Islands, alongside seagrass meadows, mangroves, rocky shores, reef fish, seahorses, giant clams, sharks, sponges, and critically endangered hawksbill turtles. Among them are remarkable stories of resilience: the rare Neptune’s Cup sponge, once thought globally extinct, has been rediscovered in Singapore’s waters, while Small Sister’s Island is home to Singapore’s first and only turtle hatchery, where hawksbill turtle nests are relocated to for protected incubation and hatching. The Southern Islands are especially significant not only for the diversity within the Hope Spot, but also for their location. Just minutes from downtown Singapore, these reefs persist alongside shipping lanes, coastal infrastructure, and heavily used marine spaces. Research shows the reefs around Sisters’ Islands function as important source reefs, releasing coral larvae that may help replenish connected habitats elsewhere in the Singapore Strait. The Southern Islands offer a compelling model for how growing coastal cities can make space for biodiversity and build resilience into the future. The Hope Spot is championed by Friends of Marine Park (FMP), a multi-stakeholder network that brings together more than 60 representatives and organisations from civil society, academia, government, industry, education, and the wider community. FMP co-chairs Sam Shu Qin, a marine conservationist and educator focused on coral reef restoration and ocean literacy, and Dr. Jani Tanzil, a marine ecologist and Facility Director of the St. John’s Island National Marine Laboratory, lead the Hope Spot. The nomination itself grew from that community. In March 2025, 42 stakeholders representing 16 organisations gathered at a Friends of Marine Park meeting where the proposal to pursue Hope Spot recognition received strong support. Emeritus Professor Chou Loke Ming, a pioneer of coral reef research and conservation in Singapore, captured the determination behind that work, stating: “Our reefs have not given up; why should we?” The Southern Islands already benefit from legal protection through Sisters’ Islands Marine Park, which is managed by Singapore’s National Parks Board. While Hope Spot recognition does not create additional regulations or legal protections, it provides greater international visibility and a platform to build momentum around Singapore’s marine community aspirations. Friends of Marine Park has developed a three-year vision centred on strengthening community participation, expanding education and citizen science, developing youth leadership, supporting research and reef restoration, securing sustainable funding, and building support for stronger and expanded marine protection in Singapore. Work is already underway. Annual coral monitoring, community clean-ups, research programmes, and educational initiatives continue across the marine park. Singapore’s largest artificial reef garden has been installed at Sisters’ Islands Marine Park under the Grow-a-Reef Garden Initiative, and is expected to contribute approximately 1000 square metres of additional reef habitat by 2030. In one of the world’s most densely populated and busiest coastal environments, the Southern Islands Hope Spot carries a simple but powerful message: there is still space for nature, and communities can choose to protect it together. Thousands of kilometres away, another of the world’s busiest maritime crossroads has also earned Hope Spot recognition, this time one that stretches across national borders. Mission Blue has designated the Strait of Sicily and Tunisian Plateau as a new Hope Spot, championed by WWF Mediterranean Marine Initiative, bringing global recognition to a marine ecosystem where extraordinary biodiversity, cultures, economies and nations converge. Positioned between the eastern and western Mediterranean basins, the Strait is a vital ecological corridor and one of the region’s most important biodiversity hotspots. It is also a strategic maritime crossroads connecting Europe and North Africa, shaped by fisheries, shipping, energy infrastructure, trade, culture, and human movement. “The ocean does not recognise the lines we draw on maps. Whales, sharks, turtles and tuna move through these waters as one connected system. The Strait of Sicily and Tunisian Plateau Hope Spot reminds us that protecting the ocean requires us to work the same way: together, across boundaries. This new Hope Spot is a source of hope for the Mediterranean and a call to turn knowledge into action.” — Dr. Sylvia Earle, CEO & Founder of Mission Blue The Strait of Sicily and Tunisian Plateau, newly named a Hope Spot championed by WWF Mediterranean Marine Initiative, spans just over 114,000 square kilometers of seagrass meadows, coralligenous reefs, and deep-sea coral supporting fin whales, loggerhead turtles, bluefin tuna, and 32 species of sharks and rays. Photo by Simone Niedermueller, courtesy of Mission Blue . Covering just over 114,000 square kilometers, the Hope Spot encompasses a remarkable range of habitats. Important oceanographic processes, including upwelling, create nutrient-rich waters that support Posidonia oceanica seagrass meadows, coralligenous reefs, maërl beds and deep-sea coral ecosystems. These habitats provide critical feeding, breeding, nursery, and migratory grounds for a wide variety of marine life, including fin whales, sperm whales, bottlenose dolphins, loggerhead sea turtles, bluefin tuna, and seabirds. The Strait is especially important for sharks and rays, supporting 32 species and earning recognition as an Important Shark and Ray Area for its exceptional elasmobranch diversity. Marine ecosystems do not recognise political borders. The Strait connects waters associated with Italy, Malta, and Tunisia, while wildlife, currents and ecological processes move freely between jurisdictions. That makes cooperation essential to its long-term protection and sustainable management. Giuseppe Di Carlo, Director of the WWF Mediterranean Marine Initiative, described the Strait as one of the clearest expressions of a shared Mediterranean future, where marine wildlife, trade routes, energy corridors and cultures converge. He said the designation offers Italy, Malta, and Tunisia a chance to show how countries can work together to safeguard a shared natural heritage, making the Strait a symbol of regional cooperation, resilience and hope. The designation builds on years of scientific research and conservation work already underway across the region. Since 2023, WWF Marine Mediterranean and its partners have brought together science, policy, and stakeholder engagement to identify conservation priorities and lay the foundations for a more coordinated approach across the Strait. The need for that cooperation is growing. The Strait faces mounting pressures from intensive fishing, maritime traffic, pollution, offshore development, habitat degradation, and climate change. These pressures do not stop at national borders, yet existing protections remain fragmented across jurisdictions and sectors. Hope Spot recognition does not create new regulations or legal protections. Instead, it adds visibility, momentum, and a shared platform for the work already underway: helping make connections around a common vision for the Strait. The next chapter moves from recognition to coordinated protection and management. One pathway being advanced is a proposed Specially Protected Area of Mediterranean Importance (SPAMI) under the Barcelona Convention, which could provide a framework for countries to work together at the ecosystem scale. The Strait of Sicily and Tunisian Plateau Hope Spot is a beacon of hope for the Mediterranean: a place of exceptional biodiversity, shared stewardship and international cooperation, where protecting one sea can benefit nature, people and generations to come. items.descriptionOriginal: The shame belongs to stigma, not to the person asking for help. “Just eat less.” “Move more.” “You need more discipline.” Is weight mainly the result of personal choices? Not quite. Choices matter, but they operate within biology, genetics, appetite, environment, health conditions and access to support. Why does that distinction matter? Because blame can delay care. Obesity is recognised as a chronic, complex and relapsing disease. A better conversation doesn’t ask, “Why can’t you control your weight?” It asks how weight may be affecting health, and what realistic, evidence-led management support is available. So keep building habits that support you: balanced meals, regular movement, strength activity and good sleep. And speak to a qualified doctor about what support is appropriate for you. Asking for medical help is responsible care, not weakness, failure or cheating. Talk to a qualified doctor about your weight-management needs. This is general information, not a diagnosis or medical advice. #CountWhatMatters #WeightStigma #Obesity #WeightManagement #HealthNotJudgement [weight is not a character test, weight stigma, obesity is a chronic disease, willpower and weight, weight management support India]

items.descriptionOriginal: P arc des Madelinots, a humble wedge of green space in the Verdun borough of Montreal, is not in the most tranquil of settings. The 6,500-square-foot pocket park sits beside a busy junction and is flanked on two sides by roads often filled with cars. For years, locals in the historically working-class neighborhood had to deal with the noise of constant passing vehicle traffic while trying to relax, meet with friends, play with their kids or, indeed, do anything else in this outdoor community space. But today, Parc des Madelinots is bathed in a very different kind of sound: the lap of ocean waves, dulcet bird calls and the crunch of sand underfoot. Reasons to Be Cheerful · Parc des Madelinots Soundscape It’s not because a beach has suddenly arrived in Verdun. The sounds are recordings being broadcast in an attempt to reshape urban noise, fighting sound with sound in a constructive way to reduce noise-induced disturbance, reinvigorate the use of the public space and even preserve cultural memory for displaced communities. “Sound is more than just noise, it can be a powerful resource,” says Catherine Guastavino, a professor at McGill University and principal investigator of Sounds in the City , a research team that is one of the collaborators on Les Madelinéennes , the sonic project in Parc des Madelinots. “We can use sounds to improve people’s experience of places.” A field recording session at the Parc des Madelinots. Credit: Paysages During the course of the 20th century, many inhabitants of the Magdalen Islands, a remote archipelago in eastern Canada, were forced to relocate to Montreal, largely in search of work. Many of them ended up in the Verdun district, which today has the largest community of madelinots outside of the islands. Yet this highly urbanized area has a problem: It’s noisy and a far cry from the islanders’ former home. So Guastavino’s team joined forces with France’s Ircam , the Institute for Research and Coordination in Acoustics/Music — one of the world’s largest public research centers dedicated to both musical expression and scientific research — and Paysages , a Montreal-based studio specializing in immersive installations, to create a more agreeable and “soothing” atmosphere in the Parc des Madelinots. This was done while at the same time paying homage to and evoking the cultural heritage of the Magdalen Islands’ diaspora. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] The installation consists of four minimalist, mounted speakers, set up in 2023, that play field recordings taken on the Magdalen Islands by Canadian sound artist Charles Montambault. The idea is that playing these natural sounds in urban areas can make them more relaxing, particularly when the sounds are familiar to residents. This method — actively cultivating the balance of sounds that are heard in any given space — is known as soundscaping. “We wanted to investigate how these coastal sounds could change the mood of the park, which had been mostly used as a place of transit,” says Valérian Fraisse, a soundscape researcher who helped prototype the installation. Urban areas are often noisy due to road traffic, construction, large cultural events and other factors. The impact of chronic noise exposure on human health is well-documented , from sleep disruption to reduced concentration and even cardiovascular disease, and cities have belatedly begun to take action. The Montreal project is part of a new wave of experiments looking to harness the power of sound rather than simply blot it out. “Sound is typically underused, it’s often considered as noise pollution,” says Guastavino. “There are detrimental impacts of noise exposure and I’m not playing that down. But sound can enhance the quality of urban experience.” A speaker (center) in Parc des Madelinots as part of the Les Madelinéennes sonic project. Credit: Paysages While the field of urban soundscaping is still emerging, similar yet simpler methods have long been used in public and private spaces, such as positioning park benches far from roads or playing music in elevators. But a growing number of innovative projects are sprouting up across the world. In Antwerp, Belgium, for example, “noise-canceling” fountains have been deployed to replace unwanted background noise like traffic. In Warsaw’s main train station, a set of stairs has been turned into giant interactive piano keys , creating a playful public space. Dating back further, Japan’s metro stations have long played out Hassha-merodii chimes to induce calm and prevent rushing, among other functions. For soundscaping to be effective it must take into account the specific contexts of each site, according to André Fiebig, a researcher and head of the working group on Psychoacoustics and Noise Effects at the Technical University of Berlin. “The solution can’t be to play sounds everywhere,” he says. “It needs to be adequate, appropriate and fit to the place.” The impact of a soundscape depends a lot on what Fiebig calls “psychoacoustic” qualities, such as how people perceive the source of noise. “People will complain about sightseeing buses, but almost never public buses,” he says. Ocean waves are usually considered relaxing, elaborates Fiebig, but if they are played everywhere then their impact lessens. And there are plenty of varieties of sound, not only loud and quiet, but sharp and subtle, strange, exciting and surprising, he adds. Soundscaper Fraisse agrees: “I don’t think there’s a universal approach we can apply to every space.” In the case of Les Madelinéennes , collaboration with residents in the development phase was important, though those involved admit it could have been more integrated. The process involved plenty of trial and error, says Fraisse, and for the first few weeks many residents didn’t even realize the installation was there. Indeed, the project was notably challenging since the park is at the intersection of roads. “An interesting result was the potential confusion,” he says. “The sound of waves could be mixed up with traffic noise.” But Fraisse, who is currently developing a methodology for creating effective sound installations, including acoustic measurement and user feedback surveys , helped adapt the sound frequency ranges so that it wasn’t mistaken for traffic, and toned down the use of boat horns, which while authentic weren’t perceived as relaxing. Reasons to Be Cheerful · Parc des Madelinots Soundscape with Horn Meanwhile, the seagull squawks weren’t quite as evocative of home as hoped — there’s plenty of them in Montreal already, and they can often be a nuisance. “That’s why it’s so important to get feedback, to design site-specific interventions with people from the place itself,” says Fraisse. Reasons to Be Cheerful · Parc des Madelinots Soundscape with Seagulls Emilie Bourgey, a resident of Verdun who was not involved in the survey, says that in the past she would not regularly go to the Parc des Madelinots due to the noise of the vehicle traffic. At times, she might briefly sit on a bench and look at the trees. But she discovered the sound installation in the summer of 2025 when walking near the kids’ play area, and that transformed her experience of the space. “I love the installation, the sound of waves, the birds, it’s very rejuvenating,” says Bourgey. “I come here specifically for the boost it gives me afterwards.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime A growing body of research is echoing the benefits of soundscapes. A review of 22 academic studies, published in 2026, found that natural soundscapes in urban areas “were consistently associated with improved mental health outcomes.” In 2024, a study of 2,000 passengers by British train operator South Western Railway found that natural sounds such as birdsong, rivers and rainfall reduced passenger stress levels by 35 percent. The Montreal installation, initially a pilot, has since become permanent. And the team wants to take the collaborative aspect to the next level. Instead of simply asking residents to evaluate sounds, it plans to involve them in the creation and selection of sounds next year as part of a third iteration of the project. “We have to try to understand their logic, what they prefer, and then try to find solutions,” says Fiebig. “It shouldn’t be decided from the top, it should be about co-creation, close cooperation between the locals and those running the project.” The post Montreal Is Harnessing Soothing Ocean Sounds to Combat Traffic Noise appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: At the height of a Saturday dinner rush in Singapore, a coffee shop server named Lau Guat Toh spotted an unattended bag and did what came naturally to her - she protected it, placed it under a security camera, and waited. Inside was $20,000 in cash, enough to rattle most people, but Lau and her colleagues "did not dare touch" it, a detail that says more about their character than any declaration of honesty could. The bag's owner, a noodle manufacturer who had rushed off to a friend's wake, returned at 11pm simply trying his luck, and found everything intact. What lingers in the story is the quiet ecosystem of goodness surrounding the moment: a boss who had spent his evening delivering donated soup to elderly residents, a customer whose first response to losing a fortune was not panic but acceptance, and a server who plans to keep her $200 reward as a souvenir rather than spend it. "If something is meant to come, it will come," said the man who lost the money - and somehow, in this small coffee shop in Bedok, it did.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Rangers Gain New Tools for Protecting Whale Sharks in the Maldives Reading Time: 3 minutes Rangers protecting whale sharks in the Maldives now have new tools to help manage heavy tourism and boat traffic in the South Ari Marine Protected Area. Protecting whale sharks in the Maldives has a new set of tools. In August 2026, rangers at the South Ari Marine Protected Area (SAMPA) received new equipment. Thermal cameras, body cameras, and a vessel-tracking device now help them enforce rules in busy waters. Tech4Nature , a partnership between the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and Huawei, provided the tools. The program, part of Huawei’s Tech4All initiative, helps protected areas use technology to meet global management standards. Designated in 2009, South Ari is the Maldives’ largest marine protected area. It covers about 5,600 hectares, nearly the size of Manhattan. Whale sharks gather there all year, making it a site of global importance for the species. Researchers have identified more than 910 whale sharks in the Maldives since 2006, mostly in South Ari. Most are young males that use the area to feed and grow. Whale sharks are the largest fish in the ocean and are listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List. These sharks draw more than 65,000 visitors a year, or about 180 every day. A 2014 study valued South Ari’s whale shark tourism at USD 9.4 million in 2013 alone. The same boats that bring that income also pose a serious threat. Whale sharks feed on plankton near the surface, where visitors can easily see them. That same habit puts them in the path of passing boats. A 2021 study in Scientific Reports found that 61% of South Ari’s whale sharks suffered major boat-strike injuries. Injured sharks tended to stay in the area longer, likely to heal in warm, food-rich water. However, staying put may mean fewer trips to breeding grounds. The researchers also pointed to a gap in protecting whale sharks in the Maldives. At the time, the area’s boating rules were suggestions, with little enforcement. SAMPA ranger Ali Gasim lists speeding vessels, crowding, and light pollution among the main problems. Speeding boats are the same risk the 2021 study linked to injuries. With limited resources, his team struggles to monitor such a large stretch of ocean. Protecting whale sharks in the Maldives remains difficult because boating rules in the area were once only suggestions with little enforcement, and SAMPA rangers, working with limited resources, struggle to monitor a large stretch of ocean while speeding vessels, crowding, and light pollution persist. Photo by Derek Keats on Pexels. Tech4Nature began by measuring those gaps. In April 2026, the team ran a baseline review with the IUCN Green List Self-Assessment Tool. The IUCN Green List is a global standard for well-managed protected areas. That review confirmed two needs: more operational capacity and stronger day-to-day enforcement. Each piece of new equipment was chosen to meet them. A vessel-mounted thermal camera detects heat, so rangers can spot boats after dark. A vessel tracking device helps them follow boat movements across the protected area. Together, these tools extend patrols into hours and places that were hard to watch before. Body cameras let rangers record encounters and collect evidence of violations. A telephoto lens lets rangers document sharks and vessels from a distance. Clear records make it much easier to take action against boats that speed or crowd an animal. Rangers completed introductory training and field tests in August 2026. The sessions covered camera use and maintenance, and how to fit the tools into existing patrol routines. Protecting whale sharks in the Maldives also depends on partners who can act on rangers’ records. The project works with the Maldives Ministry of Climate Change, Environment and Energy and the Maldives Police Service. Maldives Whale Shark Research and the Big Fish Network also contribute. Founded in 2013, Maldives Whale Shark Research tracks individual sharks over time. Each whale shark has a unique pattern of spots behind its gills that photos can identify. Divers and tourists can add their own photos to Wildbook for Whale Sharks, a global online database. That long-term record is key to measuring progress in protecting whale sharks in the Maldives. It can show whether new injuries become less common as enforcement improves. Muhusina Abdul Rahman, director of the Protected Areas Section, says innovation is essential where marine park resources are limited. Najfa Shaheem Razee, who manages the Maldives Country Program, says the project links real management needs with targeted support. The project will continue to support monitoring and data collection in South Ari. The 2014 economic study had already called for licensed operators, a code of conduct, and GPS logbooks for boats. The new tools bring several of those ideas within reach. Protecting whale sharks in the Maldives has always meant managing boats and people, not just sharks. With better tools , a small ranger team can now see more and act faster. If injuries fall, South Ari could become a model for other whale shark sites. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The best holiday parties tend to be the ones where nobody thinks about the hosting at all. Guests walk in, find a spot for their coat, settle in with a plate and a drink, and the evening carries them along. When something’s slightly off, though, they feel it long before they’d ever say it out loud. A guest who can’t hear the person next to them, or who’s stuck eating bread rolls all night because everything else has nuts in it, probably won’t complain. They’ll just leave a little earlier than they planned. The good news is that most of these little snags are easy to catch if you picture the evening from your guests’ side of the door. So let’s walk through it the way they will, from the moment they pull up to the moment they say goodbye. Before holiday guests arrive A clean home where it counts First impressions start at the entryway. Clutter underfoot or a sink full of dishes can make guests more focused on where to step than on catching up with each other. You don’t need a spotless house, though. Rooms that will stay closed can wait. Put your energy into the spaces people will use, like the bathroom, kitchen, and living room, plus the guest room if anyone’s staying over. Spreading the cleaning across a few days instead of saving it all for the night before keeps you from running on fumes when the doorbell rings. Parking, coats and the weather Even a beautifully decorated party can feel disorganized if guests circle the block looking for a parking spot or end up holding their coats for the first half hour. A short message a few days ahead covering where to park and what to expect when they arrive takes the guesswork out of it. If you live somewhere with snow or ice, it helps to have a backup plan ready in case the weather turns on the day. Food everyone can eat Nobody wants to be the guest pushing food around a plate because of an allergy the host didn’t know about. Before you settle on a menu, send a quick note asking whether anyone has dietary needs. Even if no one replies with anything, having a few dishes that happen to be gluten-free, vegan, or nut-free is an easy way to make sure no one goes hungry. Making holiday guests comfortable once the party starts Room to move around Every home has its own quirks, and the layout shapes how comfortable people feel once they’re inside. Before the party, take a slow lap through your space as if you’d never seen it. Where will people gather? Is the buffet in a spot that blocks the hallway? Is there somewhere to sit near the food? Shumaila Panhwar , a hosting professional, recommends exactly that kind of walkthrough. “When you walk through the space from the perspective of the guests and their experience, it makes it easier to determine placement of items and what makes sense best for flow,” she advises. Music that stays in the background A festive playlist does wonders for the mood, right up until people have to lean in and shout to hear each other. Keep the volume low enough that conversation comes first. Your neighbors will appreciate it too, and nothing ends a party faster than a noise complaint. Being a present host Let yourself enjoy it Here’s the one that catches even the most organized hosts. It’s easy to spend the whole evening refilling bowls and checking the oven, but your guests came to see you. Your presence matters most when people are meeting for the first time and could use an introduction to get a conversation going. Making a plan the night before and running through it once can help a lot. When you know everything is ready, it gets easier to set down the serving spoon, pour yourself a glass of something, and join the people you invited, which, when you think about it, is what made you want to host in the first place. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post 6 hosting habits that leave holiday guests feeling uneasy (and how to avoid them) first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A cell therapy built to fight cancer is helping people with stiff person syndrome get back on their feet. In an early trial led by neurologists at Mayo Clinic, patients who had needed family members to help them walk and handle daily tasks regained enough function to return to work, exercise, and hobbies after a single round of CAR-T cell therapy. The results, published in JAMA Neurology , point to a treatment that targets the root of the disease instead of only easing its symptoms. A rare disease with no cure What stiff person syndrome does to the body Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is a rare autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the central nervous system. The result can be severe rigidity throughout the body, painful muscle spasms, and frequent falls. Decades of research have produced treatments that can soften symptoms, but none that cure it. The condition drew global attention in December 2022, when singer Céline Dion revealed her diagnosis . In an Instagram video, she said it affected “every aspect of my daily life,” including her ability to sing. How CAR-T works against stiff person syndrome CAR-T therapy is already an established treatment for some blood cancers. Doctors extract a patient’s T cells, a type of immune cell, and engineer them in a lab to seek out and destroy specific targets. For this trial, the cells were redesigned to eliminate the immune cells that drive SPS, using a CD19-targeted therapy called mivocabtagene autoleucel. Each participant received a single treatment, and the study ran across three sites, Mayo Clinic among them. Dr. Anastasia Zekeridou , a neurologist and researcher at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, said the scale of the response stood out. “What was most striking was the degree of improvement we saw in some patients,” she said. “With existing treatments, we may be able to improve symptoms but we very rarely see patients return to their previous level of function.” Patients back at work and on the treadmill Jonathan Walden: hunting and fishing again Before the trial, Jonathan Walden relied on his family for help with walking and basic daily tasks. He has since returned to his job. “I can go to work every single day. I can do everything I did before. I go hunting; I can go fishing,” he said. “I have not had one episode since receiving treatment.” Shari St. Germain: seven minutes on a treadmill Shari St. Germain’s illness progressed from severe leg cramps and trouble walking to rigid muscles and falls. After CAR-T, she said, each day has felt “better and better.” One morning she felt well enough to try the treadmill. “My husband comes running in because I’m crying and he’s like: ‘Are you OK?’ And I’m like: ‘I just walked for seven minutes on the treadmill,'” she said. Next questions for CAR-T in neurology Will the improvements last? The researchers are clear that this is early evidence from a small, nonrandomized trial, and that larger studies are needed. “These early results are very encouraging and the key question now is whether those improvements will be sustained over time,” Zekeridou said. Beyond blood cancer Dr. Sean Pittock, who chairs the department of neurology at Mayo Clinic, sees a wider opening. “CAR-T therapy has already transformed the treatment of some cancers, and we are now beginning to see its potential in autoimmune neurologic diseases,” he said, adding that the results offer hope for other immune-mediated neurologic conditions with few effective options. Yasmin Sheikh, head of policy and public affairs at the UK blood cancer charity Anthony Nolan, which was not involved in the trial, called the research “an exciting development” and more evidence that CAR-T could reach well beyond blood cancer. If the gains hold in larger trials, people with stiff person syndrome could have something they have never had before: a treatment aimed at giving them back the lives the disease took, not just making those lives easier to manage. items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have long used chemogenetics to study brains in the lab. A pilot trial for seizures is its first leap into medicine. Flashing lights. Buzzing noises. A sudden wave of fear. For some people with epilepsy, these sensations herald an oncoming seizure. Drugs can keep some seizures at bay, but over 30 percent of patients don’t respond to them, a statistic that hasn’t budged in decades. Frequent, uncontrolled seizures rob people of a normal life. They can’t drive or swim alone. Some struggle to stay in school, hold down jobs, or maintain relationships. And despite growing public awareness, stigma lingers. For people with severe drug-resistant epilepsy, surgery is an option. If the seizures are associated with a local brain region, doctors can remove the tissue. It’s a drastic operation, but it isn’t rare. In 2024, over 2,000 patients elected to undergo the procedure. Depending on the brain region removed, surgery can control seizures in nearly 70 percent of patients, but they risk losing memory, language, and other cognitive abilities. A new gene therapy could offer an alternative. In a clinical trial , three men who had lived with epilepsy for at least a decade saw monthly seizures drop over 90 percent. One remained seizure-free for a year. In the trial, the team shuttled a gene into a small patch of the hippocampus, the source of their seizures. The gene produces a kind of protein “dimmer switch” in neurons. Normally silent, the protein springs into action when activated by an FDA-approved drug, allowing scientists to dial down the region’s electrical activity rather than shutting it off completely—something that’s not possible with current treatments. The technology, called chemogenetics, has been a staple of animal research in neuroscience. The findings, though early, suggest it could finally make the leap into human medicine. “It certainly has caused a lot of excitement in the field,” said Dimitri Kullmann at University College London to Chemical & Engineering News , who was not involved in the study. Chemical Romance Intricate webs of neurons underlie every brain function. Our ability to feel, move, remember, and reason all stem from electrical and chemical signals that wire brain cells into circuits. It’s a delicate balance. Some neurons release chemicals that fire up their neighbors; others dampen them. In epilepsy, this goes awry. The causes are plenty. Genetic mutations can disrupt how neurons develop or function. Brain injuries, tumors, stroke, and infections can also fuel the condition. In some frustrating cases, the culprit remains unknown. Rebalancing these circuits could tame runaway seizures. Most antiseizure drugs prevent neurons from firing too rapidly or boosting inhibitory chemical signals. But medication is a Band-Aid, not a cure. Because the drugs flood the whole brain, they can trigger fatigue, dizziness, mood swings, and sometimes more serious side effects , including liver or heart problems. Dampening electrical activity at the source could be a better bet. Around two decades ago, an emerging technology called chemogenetics first amazed neuroscientists with its precise control of single neurons. The technology relies on two parts: gene therapy and a drug. First, an engineered virus delivers a gene encoding a designer receptor into targeted neurons. The receptor is silent until a specific drug activates it. By adjusting the drug’s dose, scientists can fine tune the activity of modified neurons. Rather than simply flicking neurons on or off, the approach is flexible and targeted. Chemogenetics soon caught the attention of epilepsy researchers. In 2019, a team at Ghent University in Belgium tested the method in mice with seizures originating in the hippocampus. They delivered a designer receptor called hMADi to the region. A single dose of clozapine, an FDA-approved antipsychotic, controlled seizures for at least 15 hours. With repeated treatment, seizures nearly vanished. A subsequent study in monkeys also dramatically slashed seizures. Given these encouraging findings, some researchers were ready to take the next step. “I think scientists like me felt like, ‘Why haven’t we tried it in humans yet?’” said study author Minmin Luo at the Chinese Institute for Brain Research. Restoring Balance The trial enrolled three men under 40 diagnosed with epilepsy for 10 to 25 years. All had tried at least two antiseizure medications without success. Brain scans traced their seizures to a scarred hippocampus on one side of the brain. The same structure on the other side remained healthy. Despite their long history of epilepsy, none showed notable signs of cognitive troubles. Similar to previous work, the team delivered a gene encoding the hMADi receptor into the damaged region of each patient’s hippocampus in a series of three shots. A dye mixed with the therapy confirmed it reached nearly the entire region in two patients and spread slightly beyond it in the third. The infusion took roughly two hours. Two weeks later, the men began taking clozapine pills every eight hours. After five months, their average monthly seizure count had dropped from roughly four to nearly zero. Brain recordings also showed far fewer epilepsy-related electrical spikes, and their damaged hippocampuses increased metabolism, though levels remained below those in the region’s healthy counterpart. The benefits lasted. In check-ups throughout the following year, two patients remained seizure-free. The third experienced two “breakthrough” seizures after an unexpected interruption in medication, but the seizures stopped once he restarted the drug regime. All three participants also reported improved quality of life. The study’s main goal, however, was to gauge safety. The viral carrier has a relatively established safety record, but high doses have been linked to severe immune reactions and even deaths . Delivering the therapy directly into brain tissue requires far smaller doses than when injected into the bloodstream and perhaps, counterintuitively, could be safer overall. Blood tests, brain scans, and other assessments find no major side effects. One patient experienced a temporary rise in liver enzymes, a sign of liver stress, but levels returned to normal without intervention. The team plans to expand the trial, but there are plenty of unsolved questions. All three men continued taking their existing antiseizure medications throughout the trial, making it difficult to isolate the treatment’s effects. For example, could clozapine have somehow synergized with those medications to reduce seizure counts? The study was also open-label, without a placebo control. And clozapine, when taken at high doses, carries risks of heart and other problems , though the doses given here were much lower than those used in psychiatric disorders. Whether chemogenetics can deliver lasting seizure relief in larger groups remains to be seen. But its debut in human medicine is a hopeful glimpse of what’s possible, not just for epilepsy, but potentially for addiction, mood disorders, and other neurological conditions involving unbalanced brain circuits too. “These findings offer initial proof of concept,” the team wrote. The post Novel Gene Therapy Nearly Erases ‘Drug Resistant’ Seizures appeared first on SingularityHub .

items.descriptionOriginal: Wind turbines are designed to last for 20–25 years. By that measure, turbines around the world are an elderly lot. In the US alone, 7,500 wind turbines are at least 20 years old . As these clean energy-generating behemoths approach the end of their lives , their green reputation gets tainted. That’s because their large blades end up in landfills. Made to withstand the elements, turbine blades are so durable that breaking them down to recycle them is also not easy. But researchers at Tsinghua University have found a straightforward way to breathe new life into wind turbine blades. Their method turns old blades into two valuable manufacturing materials that can improve the mechanical and thermal properties of new blades. This new approach cuts greenhouse gas emissions by 83–92% compared to present-day recycling technique. The results can be found in the journal Chem Circularity . Wind turbine blades are made of tiny glass fibers in a resin that is made of chains that are linked closely. The fibers are difficult to separate from the resin for recycling. Existing recycling methods require rely on breaking down the resin with heat or chemical solvents. Besides consuming a lot of energy and producing chemical waste, these processes weaken the fibers and results in low-value materials. The Tsinghua team ground blade waste into powder and mixed it with carbon black. Then they place the mixture between electrodes and blast it with short intense pulses of electricity, using a technique called Flash Joule Heating. Therein lies a massive opportunity to decarbonize the grid. At these blistering temperatures, carbon reacts with silica to form silicon carbide, which is a tough, heat-resistant compound. Carbon atoms also reorganize into a one atom-thick lattice with a honeycomb structure, called graphene. Graphene, a material whose discoverers garnered the Nobel Prize, is known for its strength and ability to conduct heat and electricity. The process converted close to 60% of the mixture into a silicon carbide–graphene composite made up of 34% silicon carbide and 66% graphene. The researchers then added this composite to fresh epoxy resin for making new blades. Just 0.3% by weight of the additive made the new resin stiffer and stronger, which should increase lifetime of new blades. The researchers’ calculations also show that at commercial scale the new blade recycling approach could turn a profit of about $80 per ton of material because the recovered silicon carbide and graphene are valuable. Heat and chemical-based recycling methods, by comparison, cost $460 per ton and $1,800 per ton respectively, they say. “Many emerging waste streams, including aerospace composites, automotive lightweight structures, electronic encapsulants, and fiber-reinforced construction materials, share similar challenges,” the team writes in the paper. Their approach hints at a way to deal with those waste streams. The team is now working on ways to scale up their process. Source: Hao Bi et al. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Trust and Climate-Smart Agriculture Scaling Depend More on Neighbors Than Institutions, Study Finds Reading Time: 3 minutes A study of 514 Central American farmers found that trust and climate-smart agriculture scaling are closely linked, with relationships with neighbors mattering more than trust in outside organizations. Trust and climate-smart agriculture scaling have long been treated as separate concerns, one social, one technical. New research published in Agricultural Systems directly challenges that separation, showing that farmer-to-farmer relationships shape whether climate innovations spread at all, regardless of how well-designed they are on paper. Researchers from the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT, the University of Copenhagen, and the Gates Foundation analyzed data from 514 smallholder farmers participating in Climate-Smart Villages, known locally as Territorios Sostenibles Adaptados al Clima, across Guatemala and Honduras. The study examined how different dimensions of social capital influence knowledge sharing about climate-smart practices, and what that process reveals about the earliest stages of responsible scaling. The findings reframe how funders and policymakers should evaluate trust and the scaling of climate-smart agriculture. Success is traditionally measured only after an innovation has already reached large numbers of adopters. This study instead focuses on an earlier moment: when farmers first share experiences, discuss new practices, raise questions, and learn from one another, long before adoption becomes visible at any meaningful scale. Trust among farmers emerged as the single most consistent factor enabling knowledge sharing. When farmers trust one another, they are much more likely to share experiences, discuss new practices, and learn from each other’s successes and failures. Close relationships among farmers further strengthen these learning networks, making it easier for knowledge and hands-on experience to circulate freely within a community rather than remaining isolated within individual households. Perhaps the study’s most striking finding for trust and scaling climate-smart agriculture is the role of mutual support. Researchers found that support between farmers becomes especially critical in communities where trust remains low. In these lower-trust environments, guidance, collaboration, and the exchange of practical experience help sustain knowledge flows that trust alone would otherwise fail to carry. Mutual support effectively functions as a backup mechanism, compensating for weaker social bonds that might otherwise block information sharing entirely. Trust and climate-smart agriculture scaling depend heavily on mutual support in low-trust communities, where researchers found that guidance and collaboration between farmers help sustain the flow of knowledge that institutional trust alone fails to provide. Photo by Frank Meriño on Pexels. By contrast, the research found that trust in formal organizations, whether government agencies, NGOs, or research institutions, carried notably less influence than trust built directly among farmers themselves. This distinction matters enormously for how development programs are typically designed, since many climate-smart agriculture initiatives invest heavily in institutional credibility and extension services while underinvesting in the peer networks that this study identifies as more decisive. Researchers also found a positive association between adopting climate-smart practices and knowledge sharing, reinforcing that these two processes reinforce each other rather than operating independently. A farmer observing a neighbor successfully implementing a drought-coping technique, discussing the results, adapting that practice to their own land’s specific conditions, and later sharing their experience with others exemplifies the kind of organic circulation of trust and climate-smart agriculture scaling research seeks to capture and understand. These findings carry direct implications for how governments, development organizations, and innovation programs design their interventions. The evidence suggests development organizations need to place social dynamics at the center of scaling strategies rather than treating community relationships as secondary to technical training and resource distribution. Programs that invest in building trust and facilitating informal peer networks, rather than relying solely on top-down institutional messaging, appear better positioned to achieve the kind of local ownership that sustains results over time. Trust and climate-smart agriculture scaling research also supports what the study authors describe as a responsible scaling approach, one that anticipates and manages unintended consequences before they emerge rather than addressing problems only after widespread adoption has already occurred. Understanding how knowledge circulates among farmers before adoption becomes visible allows program designers to build strategies that are more inclusive, more context-sensitive, and more attuned to the specific social fabric of the communities they aim to serve. As agrifood systems worldwide face mounting pressure to accelerate climate adaptation, this research corrects purely technical approaches to scaling innovation. The impact of any climate-smart agricultural practice depends not only on its scientific merit, but equally on farmers’ capacity to share knowledge, learn collaboratively, and build the relationships of trust that let that knowledge travel organically through a community, often well before any formal program measures success. items.descriptionOriginal: This story was originally published by Grist . Sign up for Grist’s weekly newsletter here . Doing the laundry has grown easier and more efficient over the years, yet two things have always remained the same: A washing machine needs water, and a dryer needs heat. Technology designed to clean aerospace parts reimagines the process by ditching both of those in favor of an unlikely substitute: carbon dioxide, the very gas we’re trying so hard to contain. Under pressure, CO2 becomes a low-viscosity liquid capable of penetrating fabrics and carrying away oils and grime. When depressurized, it reverts to a gas, leaving clothes clean and dry. No wastewater. No dryer. Beyond its novelty, the idea could clean up a resource-intensive chore. The average family runs roughly 300 loads a year, consuming thousands of gallons of water. And more than 80 percent of U.S. households own a dryer, with one study putting the annual CO2 emissions from machine drying alone at 27 million metric tons . Tersus Solutions’ industrial CO2 washers use high pressure to turn carbon dioxide into a liquid that can clean fabrics without water. The machines’ bulky pressure chambers, pumps, pipes and compressors illustrate the challenge appliance makers face in trying to shrink the technology for household use. Courtesy of Teresus Solutions Long confined to industrial operations, liquid-CO2 cleaning is getting a second look from appliance giants LG and Samsung — this time for the home. Still, shrinking a technology built around bulky, high-pressure machinery to fit both a laundry room and household budget is a tall order. No less challenging is doing so without washing away the environmental gains that make waterless, dryerless laundry so enticing in the first place. Just getting this far has taken decades. Hughes Aircraft developed the process in 1990 to remove grease and other contaminants from electronic components. Electrolux later pursued it as a safer alternative to solvent-based dry cleaning, though cost, complexity, and bulky equipment kept it from catching on. In 2009, Colorado-based Tersus Solutions began refining the technology and has since carved out a niche cleaning outdoor apparel and equipment, as well as firefighter gear contaminated with hazardous residues. Its machines offer a glimpse of what CO2 cleaning can do and why squeezing it into a household appliance is no simple feat. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Tersus CEO Peter Whitcomb describes the machines as “futuristic front-loading washers,” though the company’s two models dwarf those found in a typical laundromat. Each occupies a roughly 10-foot cube, with the larger unit handling up to 85 pounds of laundry, or a dozen sleeping bags. Behind a thick, submarine-like hatch, a rotating drum sits inside a pressurized chamber amid a maze of pipes, pumps and compressors. Despite the complexity, what happens inside is relatively simple. Carbon dioxide turns from gas to liquid at 900 pounds per square inch of pressure — roughly one-third of what’s inside a full scuba tank . As it circulates, filters trap the grime, which accumulates as a thick purplish sludge for disposal. When the 45-minute cycle ends, the pressure drops and liquid returns to gas, instantly drying the load. More than 90 percent of the CO2 is recaptured for the next run; the rest escapes in a smoky wisp. The process is particularly effective on firefighter gear, with tests showing an average of more than 95 percent removal of contaminants such as PAHs, potentially harmful compounds found in smoke and soot. Water-soluble stains from sweat and food can be trickier, said Chris Robbins, Tersus’ chief technology officer, occasionally requiring pretreatment — “think Tide pen, but for CO2” — or conventional washing. For most loads, however, the process eliminates water and additives alike. “We’re not using detergent, we don’t use heat,” Whitcomb said. Tersus estimates its larger machines save roughly 300 gallons of water per load compared with conventional washing. There is another potential upside, as well: By eliminating wastewater and trapping shed fibers for disposal, the process could further reduce microplastic contamination from laundry. The energy equation, however, is more complicated. A California Energy Commission demonstration with the U.S. Navy found the method used about 15 percent less energy than smaller commercial washers and dryers, yet about as much as larger industrial combinations. Tersus has found comparable performance, said Robbins. While CO2 cleaning avoids thermal drying — typically the most energy-intensive part of conventional laundry — removing impurities from the carbon dioxide for reuse requires significant power. The company is exploring more efficient ways of heating and cooling the gas, Robbins said. As for the CO2, Tersus gets it from a nearby ethanol plant, where it’s a byproduct of fermentation. That minimizes transportation needs, although purifying and liquefying it require additional energy — further complicating the calculation of the technology’s overall carbon footprint. Then there’s the question of scale: Could all that machinery — enough to fill a small bedroom — be shrunk into a household appliance? LG and Samsung are working on that. Recent patents from the companies, both of which declined to comment, tackle distinct challenges: removing stains resistant to CO2 cleaning and reducing the pressure required to make the tech work. LG’s design uses detergents and other additives to help remove water-soluble stains. Although the patent doesn’t specify a formula, a recent study found that adding isopropyl alcohol and water improved liquid carbon dioxide’s ability to remove sugars, salts and other compounds. Samsung, meanwhile, proposes combining CO2 with other solvents to bring operating pressures down to a fraction of those used in industrial machines. That could make home models more compact, though some of the mixtures include PFAS , raising questions about environmental trade-offs. Smaller, however, doesn’t necessarily mean simpler. Separating and recovering those added solvents could require still more equipment, said Eckhard Groll, head of mechanical engineering at Purdue University and an expert in CO2 refrigeration. “There’s no question” that a home version is technically feasible, he said, “but it may be very costly, the technology.” Even if the machines become affordable, the environmental benefits may not carry over, said Rainer Stamminger, a household appliance efficiency researcher at the University of Bonn. With households running just a few loads a week, pressurizing and recovering carbon dioxide could be “very inefficient just for one wash” compared to industrial machines that run continuously. The economics may be especially challenging in the U.S., where electricity is relatively cheap. Groll pointed to heat pump dryers, which use about half the energy of conventional electric models. Popular in Europe, they made up 75 percent of new dryer sales in 2020, helped by higher electricity prices that helped ease the sticker shock; meanwhile, American sales still lag . CO2 washers could as well if their efficiency comes with a hefty upfront premium. Whitcomb sees greater opportunities in commercial dry cleaning, apartment buildings and institutions, where higher volumes could justify the equipment costs — and keep the machines running often enough to take advantage of their scale. With a new facility in Calgary expanding its Colorado operations, Tersus now works with more than 40 brands and retailers, offering repairs, restoration and resale services that “complement the cleaning” to extend garment life and keep products in circulation, Whitcomb said. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Even if engineers can make a home CO2 washer affordable and efficient, they would still have to convince people to buy one. The early market for water-efficient front-load washers offers a precedent: Energy and water savings attracted some consumers, while upfront costs deterred others. Performance and convenience mattered, too, said Gwendolyn Hustvedt, a textiles and consumer sciences professor at Texas State University who studied the trend. The technology may have one big selling point, however: The clothes come out dry. Beyond saving time and hassle, skipping what Hustvedt called “cooking your clothes in a box” could help garments last longer by reducing shrinkage and wear from heat and tumbling. Whether consumers would pay a premium for those benefits is another question. Home CO2 washers still have a long way to go before they break up the familiar washer-dryer combo. But if engineers can make the physics work economically — and environmentally — at household scale, the next big thing in laundry might be one less appliance. This article originally appeared in Grist at https://grist.org/science/carbon-dioxide-is-a-climate-problem-it-might-also-be-a-laundry-solution/ . Grist is a nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to reporting on climate change. items.descriptionOriginal: Garry oak trees, home for bluebirds nested in cavities, were tended by First Nations for millennia. Without their care, 95 percent of the Garry oak ecosystem was lost to agriculture, pesticides, and urban development. Their homes gone, bluebirds left, and were declared extinct on Vancouver Island and the southern Gulf Islands. “Garry oak trees are a great source of insects,” said Jacquie Taylor, coordinator for the Cowichan Bring Back the Bluebirds Project. “They have a real biodiversity of their own, things that live in the bark and on the trees.” Saving them would help save the bluebirds. Canadians and Americans worked together, along with a military base, a slew of permits, thousands of volunteer hours, private property owners, Cowichan Tribes, and lots and lots of tiny, wriggling mealworms to help the bluebirds return. “But most noticeable is the sound: a gentle musical chortling so cheerful and soothing that it immediately banishes all thought of the ills of the world.”

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Watershed Restoration in Ethiopia Reaches First Major Milestone Reading Time: 3 minutes Watershed restoration in Ethiopia reached a new milestone as 1,000 community members planted 152,333 seedlings across four degraded micro-watersheds in the Tana Subbasin. Watershed restoration in Ethiopia reached a new milestone in July, with more than 1,000 community members planting over 150,000 tree seedlings across four degraded micro-watersheds . The effort marks ProTana’s first major field campaign, a five-year project led by the World Resources Institute and partners. Nearly half of the volunteers were women. ProTana focuses on the Tana Subbasin in Ethiopia’s Amhara Region, home to Lake Tana, the country’s largest lake and the source of the Blue Nile. The lake and its surrounding watersheds supply water for millions of people across the region. Decades of deforestation, overgrazing, and soil erosion have steadily degraded the land feeding into it. Lake Tana’s importance reaches well beyond Ethiopia’s borders. Water flowing out of the lake eventually joins the Blue Nile, which supplies a significant share of the water reaching Sudan and Egypt downstream. Keeping the watersheds that feed the lake healthy therefore affects water security across the wider Nile basin, not just the communities living closest to it. The World Resources Institute (WRI) is implementing the project alongside WaterAid Ethiopia and ORDA Ethiopia, focusing on three districts: North Mecha, Farta, and Dera. Selecting which specific watersheds to restore took months of consultation with local officials and community leaders. Criteria included erosion severity, the importance of water supply, and each community’s willingness to participate. The four selected micro-watersheds span more than 2,100 hectares combined. During July’s planting campaign, workers and volunteers put in over 152,000 seedlings, split between private agroforestry plots and communal or institutional land. Planting took place at the start of Ethiopia’s main rainy season to give seedlings the best chance of survival. Community turnout exceeded expectations, with more than 1,000 people taking part directly. Many children and young people also attended, watched the planting process, and learned why restoring the land matters for their future water security. Organizers see early engagement as key to building long-term support, since restoration work without community buy-in rarely survives past its first planting season. Watershed restoration in Ethiopia drew more than 1,000 community participants, with children and young people watching and learning alongside adults, as organizers bet that early engagement is the only way to build the long-term community buy-in that keeps restoration work alive past its first planting season. Photo by Khedir Dawed, courtesy of World Resources Institute . This campaign builds on an earlier three-year pilot in the Minzir 01 micro-watershed, part of the same broader area. That pilot showed measurable improvements in local water supply alongside benefits for nearby crop farming. ProTana now aims to apply those same lessons across a much larger area. Tree planting represents only the first phase of watershed restoration in Ethiopia under this project. Future work will include soil and water conservation measures such as terracing, check dams, and soil bunds. Regenerative agricultural practices are also planned to help households manage land more sustainably over the long term. A WRI program specialist working on the project described success as depending heavily on strong local leadership and coordination between partners. He noted that when communities see real benefits firsthand, they tend to stay far more committed to protecting restored land afterward, rather than treating conservation as an outside obligation imposed on them. According to the World Resources Institute, watershed restoration in Ethiopia fits into a broader strategy addressing water risk, climate resilience, and sustainable water governance across the country. The organization continues to monitor seedling survival through the rainy season to track how well the new plantings take hold. If ProTana’s larger rollout matches the results seen in its earlier pilot, this round of watershed restoration in Ethiopia could improve water availability and livelihoods for thousands of households in the Tana Subbasin. Much of that outcome will depend on how well new seedlings survive and how consistently local institutions keep up conservation work after the initial planting rush ends. For now, the scale of community turnout offers an early, encouraging sign that residents are ready to stay involved for the long haul. The post Watershed Restoration in Ethiopia Reaches First Major Milestone appeared first on Happy Eco News .
